about: English meaning written for this library (en-scriptures): a plain meaning of each mantra, faithful to the words, following the traditional reading (Śaṅkara's bhāṣya); a long prose mantra renders every clause in its order. [meaning, [footnotes]]

shanti.1: Om. May my limbs grow strong: speech, the life-breath, the eye,
and the ear, and my strength and all my senses too.
All is Brahman, the Absolute, taught in the Upaniṣads. May I not reject Brahman;
may Brahman not reject me. Let there be no rejection; let there be no rejection for me.
In me, who delight in that Self, the dharmas, the virtues, that the Upaniṣads teach —
may they be in me; may they be in me.
1.1.1: One should meditate on the syllable Om as the udgītha, the main part of the sāman chant, for it is with Om that one begins to chant it aloud. Here follows its explanation.
1.1.2: The earth is the essence of all these beings; water is the essence of the earth. The plants are the essence of water; man is the essence of the plants; speech is the essence of man; the ṛk, the verse, is the essence of speech; the sāman, the chant, is the essence of the ṛk; and the udgītha is the essence of the sāman.
1.1.3: This udgītha is the finest essence of all essences, the supreme, worthy of the highest place, and the eighth in this count.
1.1.4: Which, which is the ṛk? Which, which is the sāman? Which, which is the udgītha? This is now considered.
1.1.5: Speech itself is the ṛk, prāṇa, the vital breath, is the sāman, and this syllable Om is the udgītha. That, indeed, is a pair: speech and prāṇa, the ṛk and the sāman.
1.1.6: This pair is joined together in this syllable Om. When the two of a pair come together, each surely fulfils the other's desire.
1.1.7: He truly becomes a fulfiller of desires who, knowing thus, meditates on this syllable as the udgītha.
1.1.8: This syllable, truly, is the syllable of assent: whenever one assents to anything, one says just Om. And assent is itself prosperity. He truly becomes one who brings desires to fulfilment who, knowing thus, meditates on this syllable as the udgītha.
1.1.9: By it this threefold knowledge, the Vedic rite, goes on: with Om the call to the gods is given, with Om the hymn is recited, with Om the chant is sung aloud — in honour of this very syllable, by its greatness and by its essence.
1.1.10: With it both perform the rites: he who knows it thus and he who does not. But knowledge and ignorance are different. What one does with knowledge, with faith and with upaniṣad, meditation, that alone becomes the more powerful. Such, truly, is the explanation of this very syllable.
1.2.1: When the gods and the demons, both offspring of Prajāpati, fought each other, the gods took up the udgītha, thinking: With this we shall overcome them.
1.2.2: They meditated on the udgītha as the prāṇa in the nose. The demons pierced it with evil. That is why with it one smells both, the fragrant and the foul; for it is pierced by evil.
1.2.3: Then they meditated on the udgītha as speech. The demons pierced it with evil. That is why with it one speaks both, truth and untruth; for it is pierced by evil.
1.2.4: Then they meditated on the udgītha as the eye. The demons pierced it with evil. That is why with it one sees both, what is fit to be seen and what is not; for it is pierced by evil.
1.2.5: Then they meditated on the udgītha as the ear. The demons pierced it with evil. That is why with it one hears both, what is fit to be heard and what is not; for it is pierced by evil.
1.2.6: Then they meditated on the udgītha as the mind. The demons pierced it with evil. That is why with it one conceives both, what is fit to be conceived and what is not; for it is pierced by evil.
1.2.7: Then they meditated on the udgītha as this chief prāṇa, the breath in the mouth. The demons struck it and were shattered, as a clod would be shattered on striking a rock that cannot be dug.
1.2.8: Just as a clod is shattered on striking a rock that cannot be dug, so is he shattered who wishes evil to one who knows thus, and he who harms him; for such a knower is a rock that cannot be dug.
1.2.9: With it one knows neither the fragrant nor the foul, for it is free from evil. With whatever one eats and drinks through it, it sustains the other prāṇas. At the end, at death, not finding this, its food and drink, the other prāṇas depart; that is why at the end one opens the mouth wide.
1.2.10: Aṅgiras meditated on the udgītha as this prāṇa. People regard this very prāṇa as Āṅgirasa, because it is the essence (rasa) of the limbs (aṅga).
1.2.11: In the same way Bṛhaspati meditated on the udgītha as this prāṇa. People regard this very prāṇa as Bṛhaspati, for speech is bṛhatī, the great one, and this is her lord (pati).
1.2.12: In the same way Āyāsya meditated on the udgītha as this prāṇa. People regard this very prāṇa as Āyāsya, because it goes forth from the mouth (āsya).
1.2.13: In the same way Baka Dālbhya knew it. He became the udgātṛ, the chanting priest, of those holding a sacrifice in the Naimiṣa forest, and by his chanting he used to win their desires for them.
1.2.14: He truly becomes one who wins desires by his chanting who, knowing thus, meditates on this syllable as the udgītha. This is the meditation with regard to oneself (adhyātma).
1.3.1: Now with regard to the gods (adhidaivata): one should meditate on the udgītha as the sun that shines yonder. Rising, it chants aloud for all creatures; rising, it drives away darkness and fear. He who knows thus truly becomes a dispeller of fear and darkness.
1.3.2: This prāṇa and that sun are alike. This is warm, that is warm. This one they call svara, the one that goes out; that one they call svara and pratyāsvara, the one that goes out and comes back. Therefore one should meditate on the udgītha as this and as that.
1.3.3: Now, one should meditate on the udgītha as vyāna alone. The breathing out is prāṇa; the breathing in is apāna. The junction of prāṇa and apāna is vyāna, and vyāna is speech. That is why one utters speech neither breathing out nor breathing in.
1.3.4: Speech is the ṛk; that is why one utters a ṛk neither breathing out nor breathing in. The ṛk is the sāman; that is why one sings a sāman neither breathing out nor breathing in. The sāman is the udgītha; that is why one chants the udgītha neither breathing out nor breathing in.
1.3.5: So too the other deeds that need strength — kindling fire by friction, running a race to the mark, bending a strong bow — one does neither breathing out nor breathing in. For this reason one should meditate on the udgītha as vyāna alone.
1.3.6: Now one should meditate on the syllables of the name udgītha: ud, gī, tha. Prāṇa is ud, for by prāṇa one rises up (ut-tiṣṭhati). Speech is gī, for speech is called gir. Food is tha, for on food all this is established (sthita).
1.3.7: Heaven is ud, the mid-region gī, the earth tha. The sun is ud, the wind gī, fire tha. The Sāmaveda is ud, the Yajurveda gī, the Ṛgveda tha. Speech yields its milk for him, the milk that is speech's own, and he becomes rich in food and an eater of food, who, knowing thus, meditates on these syllables of the udgītha: ud, gī, tha.
1.3.8: Now the fulfilment of wishes. One should meditate on what is to be approached in thought, thus: the sāman with which he is about to praise — on that sāman he should reflect.
1.3.9: On the ṛk in which that sāman is set, on that ṛk; on the sage to whom it belongs, on that sage; on the deity he is about to praise, on that deity he should reflect.
1.3.10: On the metre in which he is about to praise, on that metre he should reflect; on the stoma, the order of the chanted hymn, with which he is about to praise, on that stoma he should reflect.
1.3.11: On the direction he is about to praise, on that direction he should reflect.
1.3.12: Last of all, coming to himself in thought, he should praise, meditating on his desire, without heedlessness. Quickly indeed will that desire be fulfilled for him, desiring which he praises — desiring which he praises.
1.4.1: One should meditate on the syllable Om as the udgītha, the main part of the sāman chant, for it is with Om that one begins to chant it aloud. Here follows its explanation.
1.4.2: The gods, afraid of death, entered the threefold knowledge, the rites of the three Vedas. They covered themselves with the metres. Because they covered (acchādayan) themselves with these, the metres are called chandas.
1.4.3: There Death saw them, as one might see a fish in water — in the ṛk, in the sāman, in the yajus. Knowing this, they rose up out of the ṛk, the sāman and the yajus, and entered the svara, the sound Om, alone.
1.4.4: When one masters a ṛk, one sounds Om with a sustained note; so with a sāman, so with a yajus. This syllable is the svara; it is the immortal, the fearless. Having entered it, the gods became immortal and fearless.
1.4.5: He who, knowing thus, praises this syllable enters this very syllable, the svara, immortal and fearless; having entered it, he becomes immortal as the gods are immortal.
1.5.1: Now, what is the udgītha, the chief part of the sāman chant, is the praṇava, the syllable Om; and what is the praṇava is the udgītha. That sun is the udgītha, it is the praṇava, for it moves along sounding Om.
1.5.2: Kauṣītaki said to his son: It was this one, the sun, that I sang of; that is why you are my only son. Dwell again and again on the rays, as many and apart from the sun, and many sons will surely be yours. This is the meditation concerning the gods.
1.5.3: Now the meditation concerning the body: one should meditate on this chief prāṇa, the breath of life, as the udgītha, for it moves along sounding Om.
1.5.4: Kauṣītaki said to his son: It was this one, the chief prāṇa, that I sang of; that is why you are my only son. Sing of the prāṇas as many, with the thought: Many sons will surely be mine.
1.5.5: Now, what is the udgītha is the praṇava, and what is the praṇava is the udgītha: one who knows this, even from the seat of the hotṛ, the priest who recites the Ṛgveda, sets right an udgītha that was wrongly sung, sets it right.
1.6.1: This earth is the ṛk, the verse; fire is the sāman, the chant. This sāman rests upon this ṛk; therefore the sāman is sung resting upon the ṛk. The earth is sā, fire is ama: together that is sāma.
1.6.2: The mid-region is the ṛk, the wind is the sāman. This sāman rests upon this ṛk; therefore the sāman is sung resting upon the ṛk. The mid-region is sā, the wind is ama: together that is sāma.
1.6.3: The sky is the ṛk, the sun is the sāman. This sāman rests upon this ṛk; therefore the sāman is sung resting upon the ṛk. The sky is sā, the sun is ama: together that is sāma.
1.6.4: The stars are the ṛk, the moon is the sāman. This sāman rests upon this ṛk; therefore the sāman is sung resting upon the ṛk. The stars are sā, the moon is ama: together that is sāma.
1.6.5: Now, the white light of the sun is the ṛk; and the blue, deep black, is the sāman. This sāman rests upon this ṛk; therefore the sāman is sung resting upon the ṛk.
1.6.6: Now, the white light of the sun is sā, and the blue, deep black, is ama: together that is sāma. And the golden person who is seen within the sun, golden of beard and golden of hair, all golden to the very tips of his nails,
1.6.7: his two eyes are like a lotus as red as a monkey's rump. His name is Ut, for he has risen above all evils. He who knows thus surely rises above all evils.
1.6.8: The ṛk and the sāman are his two joints; therefore he is the udgītha. And for this reason the udgātṛ, the priest who sings the udgītha, bears that name, for he is the singer of this Ut. He rules over the worlds that lie beyond that sun, and over the desires of the gods. This is the meditation concerning the gods.
1.7.1: Now the meditation concerning the body: speech is the ṛk, breath is the sāman. This sāman rests upon this ṛk; therefore the sāman is sung resting upon the ṛk. Speech is sā, breath is ama: together that is sāma.
1.7.2: The eye is the ṛk, the ātman (the image seen in the eye) is the sāman. This sāman rests upon this ṛk; therefore the sāman is sung resting upon the ṛk. The eye is sā, the ātman is ama: together that is sāma.
1.7.3: The ear is the ṛk, the mind is the sāman. This sāman rests upon this ṛk; therefore the sāman is sung resting upon the ṛk. The ear is sā, the mind is ama: together that is sāma.
1.7.4: Now, the white light of the eye is the ṛk; and the blue, deep black, is the sāman. This sāman rests upon this ṛk; therefore the sāman is sung resting upon the ṛk. And the white light of the eye is sā, and the blue, deep black, is ama: together that is sāma.
1.7.5: And the person who is seen within the eye is the ṛk, he is the sāman, he is the uktha, the recited hymn, he is the yajus, he is Brahman, here the Veda. The form of this one is the form of that one in the sun; the two joints of that one are the joints of this one; the name of that one is the name of this one.
1.7.6: He rules over the worlds that lie below this one in the eye, and over the desires of men. So those who sing to the vīṇā sing of him; that is why they win wealth.
1.7.7: Now he who, knowing it thus, sings the sāman sings of both. Through that one in the sun, becoming that very one, he gains the worlds that lie beyond it, and the desires of the gods too.
1.7.8: And through this one in the eye he gains the worlds that lie below it, and the desires of men too. Therefore an udgātṛ who knows this should say to the sacrificer:
1.7.9: What desire of yours shall I win for you by my singing? For he alone has the power to win desires by song who, knowing it thus, sings the sāman, sings the sāman.
1.8.1: There were three men skilled in the udgītha: Śilaka Śālāvatya, Caikitāyana Dālbhya and Pravāhaṇa Jaivali. They said: We are known to be skilled in the udgītha; come, let us hold a discussion on the udgītha.
1.8.2: Saying: So be it, they sat down together. Then Pravāhaṇa Jaivali said: Let the two of you, revered sirs, speak first; I will listen to the words of two brāhmaṇas as they speak.
1.8.3: Then Śilaka Śālāvatya said to Caikitāyana Dālbhya: Come, let me question you. Dālbhya said: Ask.
1.8.4: Śilaka asked: What is the support of the sāman? Dālbhya said: Tone. What is the support of tone? He said: Breath. What is the support of breath? He said: Food. What is the support of food? He said: Water.
1.8.5: What is the support of water? Dālbhya said: That world, heaven. What is the support of that world? He said: The sāman should not be carried beyond the world of heaven. We establish the sāman in the world of heaven, for the sāman is praised as heaven.
1.8.6: Śilaka Śālāvatya said to Caikitāyana Dālbhya: Dālbhya, your sāman indeed has no foundation. If someone were now to say: Your head will fall off, your head would fall off.
1.8.7: Dālbhya said: Well, let me learn this from you, sir. Śilaka said: Learn it. Dālbhya asked: What is the support of that world? Śilaka said: This world. What is the support of this world? He said: The sāman should not be carried beyond this world, the foundation. We establish the sāman in this world as its foundation, for the sāman is praised as the foundation.
1.8.8: Pravāhaṇa Jaivali said to him: Śālāvatya, your sāman indeed has an end. If someone were now to say: Your head will fall off, your head would fall off. Śālāvatya said: Well, let me learn this from you, sir. Pravāhaṇa said: Learn it.
1.9.1: Śālāvatya asked: What is the support of this world? Pravāhaṇa said: Ākāśa, space. For all these beings arise from space alone and go back into space. Space alone is greater than all these; space is the final resting place.
1.9.2: This is the udgītha that is higher than the high; it is without end. He who, knowing it thus, meditates on the udgītha as higher than the high, his life becomes higher than the high, and he wins worlds ever higher.
1.9.3: Atidhanvan Śaunaka, having taught this udgītha to Udaraśāṇḍilya, said: As long as those among your descendants know this udgītha, so long will their life in this world be higher than the high,
1.9.4: and so too their world in that other world. He who, knowing it thus, meditates on it, his life in this world becomes higher than the high, and so too his world in that other world, his world in that other world.
1.10.1: When the crops of the Kurus had been laid waste by hail, Uṣasti Cākrāyaṇa lived in dire want, with his wife who was still a young girl, in the village of an ibhya, a rich man.
1.10.2: He begged food from the rich man, who was eating coarse beans. The rich man said to him: I have no others than these, and what I have is set here before me.
1.10.3: Uṣasti said: Give me some of these. He gave them to him. The rich man said: Here is water to drink with them. Uṣasti said: Then I would have drunk what is left over by another.
1.10.4: The rich man asked: Are these beans not left over too? Uṣasti said: I would not have lived had I not eaten them; but water I can drink as I please.
1.10.5: Having eaten, he brought what remained to his wife. She had already received good alms; she took the beans from him and put them away.
1.10.6: Rising in the morning, he said: Alas, if only we could get a little food, we could earn a little wealth. That king there is going to perform a sacrifice; he would choose me for all the priestly offices.
1.10.7: His wife said to him: Here, my husband, are those very beans. He ate them and went to that sacrifice, which was then under way.
1.10.8: There he went up to the udgātṛs who were about to sing the hymns of praise in the āstāva, the place of chanting, and sat down near them. He said to the prastotṛ, the priest who sings the prastāva, the prelude:
1.10.9: Prastotṛ, if you sing the prastāva without knowing the deity that belongs to the prastāva, your head will fall off.
1.10.10: In the same way he said to the udgātṛ: Udgātṛ, if you sing the udgītha without knowing the deity that belongs to the udgītha, your head will fall off.
1.10.11: In the same way he said to the pratihartṛ, the priest who sings the pratihāra, the response: Pratihartṛ, if you sing the pratihāra without knowing the deity that belongs to the pratihāra, your head will fall off. They stopped their work and sat in silence.
1.11.1: Then the sacrificer said to him: I wish to know your reverence. He said: I am Uṣasti Cākrāyaṇa.
1.11.2: The sacrificer said: It was your reverence I searched for, for all these priestly offices; not finding your reverence, I chose others.
1.11.3: Your reverence alone shall be mine for all the priestly offices. Uṣasti said: So be it. But then let these same priests, given leave by me, sing the praises; only, as much wealth as you give them, give as much to me. The sacrificer said: So be it.
1.11.4: Then the prastotṛ came up to him and said: Your reverence told me: Prastotṛ, there is a deity joined to the prastāva, the opening part of the sāman chant; if you sing the prastāva without knowing that deity, your head will fall off. Which is that deity?
1.11.5: Uṣasti said: Prāṇa, the breath of life. All these beings enter into prāṇa alone, and out of prāṇa they rise. This is the deity joined to the prastāva. Had you sung the prastāva without knowing it, after I had told you so, your head would have fallen off.
1.11.6: Then the udgātṛ came up to him and said: Your reverence told me: Udgātṛ, there is a deity joined to the udgītha, the chief part of the chant; if you sing the udgītha without knowing that deity, your head will fall off. Which is that deity?
1.11.7: Uṣasti said: The sun. All these beings sing of the sun when he stands high. This is the deity joined to the udgītha. Had you sung the udgītha without knowing it, after I had told you so, your head would have fallen off.
1.11.8: Then the pratihartṛ came up to him and said: Your reverence told me: Pratihartṛ, there is a deity joined to the pratihāra, the part sung after the udgītha; if you sing the pratihāra without knowing that deity, your head will fall off. Which is that deity?
1.11.9: Uṣasti said: Food. All these beings live only by taking food to themselves. This is the deity joined to the pratihāra. Had you sung the pratihāra without knowing it, after I had told you so, your head would have fallen off — after I had told you so.
1.12.1: Now next, the udgītha of the dogs. Baka Dālbhya, or Glāva Maitreya, went out of the village for his Vedic recitation.
1.12.2: A white dog appeared before him. Other dogs gathered round it and said: Revered one, obtain food for us by your singing; we are hungry.
1.12.3: The white dog said to them: Gather here before me in the morning. Baka Dālbhya, or Glāva Maitreya, waited there and watched.
1.12.4: Just as the priests about to sing the praise with the Bahiṣpavamāna hymn move along holding on to one another, so the dogs moved along. Then, sitting down together, they made the sound hiṃ.
1.12.5: Om, let us eat. Om, let us drink. Om, may the god, Varuṇa, Prajāpati, Savitṛ, bring food here. Lord of food, bring food here, bring it, Om.
1.13.1: This world indeed is the syllable hāu, a stobha sung in the chant; the wind is hāi; the moon is atha. The self is iha; fire is ī.
1.13.2: The sun is ū; the invocation is e; the Viśvedevas, the All-gods, are auhoyi; Prajāpati is hiṃ; prāṇa is svara; food is yā; speech is virāj.
1.13.3: The thirteenth stobha, huṃ, is the undefined, which cannot be named as this or that, and it varies.
1.13.4: Speech yields its milk for him, the milk that is speech's own, and he becomes rich in food and an eater of food, who knows thus this upaniṣad, the secret teaching, of the sāmans — who knows the upaniṣad.
2.1.1: The meditation on the whole sāman is good. What is good, people call sāman; what is not good, asāman.
2.1.2: That is why people also say: He approached him with sāman, and by it they mean only that he approached him in a good way. And: He approached him with asāman, and by it they mean only that he approached him in a way that is not good.
2.1.3: And they also say: Ah, this is sāman for us, when what happens is good; by it they mean only: Ah, it is good. And: Alas, this is asāman for us, when what happens is not good; by it they mean only: Alas, it is not good.
2.1.4: He who, knowing this thus, meditates on the sāman as good: good dharmas, right qualities and ways, quickly come to him and are there for his enjoyment.
2.2.1: One should meditate on the fivefold sāman in the worlds. The earth is the hiṅkāra, the sound hiṃ that opens the chant. Fire is the prastāva, the mid-region the udgītha, the sun the pratihāra, heaven the nidhana, the closing part: this in the worlds going upward.
2.2.2: Now in the worlds turning back downward: heaven is the hiṅkāra, the sun the prastāva, the mid-region the udgītha, fire the pratihāra, the earth the nidhana.
2.2.3: The worlds, going upward and turning back downward, are favourable to him who, knowing this thus, meditates on the fivefold sāman in the worlds.
2.3.1: One should meditate on the fivefold sāman in rain. The wind that comes before the rain is the hiṅkāra; a cloud forms, that is the prastāva; it rains, that is the udgītha; it flashes and thunders, that is the pratihāra; it holds back the rain, that is the nidhana.
2.3.2: It rains for him, and he makes it rain, who, knowing this thus, meditates on the fivefold sāman in rain.
2.4.1: One should meditate on the fivefold sāman in all waters. When the cloud gathers, that is the hiṅkāra; when it rains, that is the prastāva; the waters that flow eastward are the udgītha; those that flow westward, the pratihāra; the ocean is the nidhana.
2.4.2: He does not die in water, and he becomes rich in water, who, knowing this thus, meditates on the fivefold sāman in all waters.
2.5.1: One should meditate on the fivefold sāman in the seasons. Spring is the hiṅkāra, summer the prastāva, the rains the udgītha, autumn the pratihāra, winter the nidhana.
2.5.2: The seasons are favourable to him, and he becomes rich in the seasons' gifts, who, knowing this thus, meditates on the fivefold sāman in the seasons.
2.6.1: One should meditate on the fivefold sāman in animals. Goats are the hiṅkāra, sheep the prastāva, cows the udgītha, horses the pratihāra, man the nidhana.
2.6.2: Animals come to be his, and he becomes rich in animals, who, knowing this thus, meditates on the fivefold sāman in animals.
2.7.1: One should meditate in the prāṇas, the powers of sense, on the fivefold sāman, each part greater than the one before. Prāṇa, the sense of smell, is the hiṅkāra, speech the prastāva, the eye the udgītha, the ear the pratihāra, the mind the nidhana. These indeed are each greater than the one before.
2.7.2: His life becomes higher than the high, and he wins worlds ever higher, who, knowing this thus, meditates in the prāṇas on the fivefold sāman, each part greater than the one before. So much for the fivefold sāman.
2.8.1: Now the sevenfold. One should meditate on the sevenfold sāman in speech. Whatever of speech is huṃ, that is the hiṅkāra; what is pra, that is the prastāva; what is ā, that is the ādi, the beginning, the syllable Om.
2.8.2: What is ut, that is the udgītha; what is prati, that is the pratihāra; what is upa, that is the upadrava, the part before the close; what is ni, that is the nidhana.
2.8.3: Speech yields its milk for him, the milk that is speech's own, and he becomes rich in food and an eater of food, who, knowing this thus, meditates on the sevenfold sāman in speech.
2.9.1: Now indeed one should meditate on yonder sun as the sevenfold sāman. He is always the same, sama, and so he is sāman. He faces me, he faces me, each one thinks, so he is the same to all, and so he is sāman.
2.9.2: One should know that all these beings depend on him. What he is before his rising, that is the hiṅkāra; on this form of his the animals depend. That is why they make the sound hiṃ, for they share in the hiṅkāra of this sāman.
2.9.3: Then what he is when he has first risen, that is the prastāva; on this form of his men depend. That is why they long for praise and long for commendation, for they share in the prastāva of this sāman.
2.9.4: Then what he is at saṅgava, the time when cows join their calves, that is the ādi; on this form of his the birds depend. That is why they fly about in the mid-air without support, holding themselves up, for they share in the ādi of this sāman.
2.9.5: Then what he is at exact midday, that is the udgītha; on this form of his the gods depend. That is why they are the best of Prajāpati's offspring, for they share in the udgītha of this sāman.
2.9.6: Then what he is after midday and before the afternoon, that is the pratihāra; on this form of his embryos depend. That is why, held up, they do not fall down, for they share in the pratihāra of this sāman.
2.9.7: Then what he is after the afternoon and before sunset, that is the upadrava; on this form of his the wild animals depend. That is why, on seeing a man, they run off to the thicket, to a hole, for they share in the upadrava of this sāman.
2.9.8: Then what he is just after sunset, that is the nidhana; on this form of his the ancestors depend. That is why people lay them down on the sacred grass, for they share in the nidhana of this sāman. Thus indeed one meditates on yonder sun as the sevenfold sāman.
2.10.1: Now, one should meditate on the sevenfold sāman, the chant, whose parts are equal in measure and which goes beyond death. The name hiṅkāra has three syllables, the name prastāva has three syllables: that is equal.
2.10.2: The name ādi has two syllables, the name pratihāra has four; when one syllable is taken from there to here, that is equal.
2.10.3: The name udgītha, the chief chant, has three syllables, the name upadrava has four. By threes they are equal, and one syllable is left over; called akṣara, it too has three syllables, so that is equal.
2.10.4: The name nidhana has three syllables; that is equal too. Together these are twenty-two syllables.
2.10.5: With twenty-one syllables one reaches the sun, for counted from here the sun yonder is the twenty-first. With the twenty-second one wins the world beyond the sun: that is nāka, where there is no pain; that is free from sorrow.
2.10.6: He gains the victory of the sun, and a victory higher than the sun's victory becomes his, who, knowing this thus, meditates on the sevenfold sāman whose parts are equal in measure and which goes beyond death; who meditates on the sāman.
2.11.1: The mind is the hiṅkāra, speech the prastāva, the eye the udgītha, the ear the pratihāra, and prāṇa, the life-breath, the nidhana. This is the Gāyatra sāman, woven into the prāṇas, the senses.
2.11.2: He who knows this Gāyatra thus, woven into the prāṇas, keeps all his senses whole, reaches the full span of life, lives brightly, becomes great in offspring and cattle, and great in fame. He should be large-hearted: that is his vow.
2.12.1: One churns the fire-sticks: that is the hiṅkāra. Smoke rises: that is the prastāva. The fire blazes: that is the udgītha. Embers form: that is the pratihāra. It begins to die down: that is the nidhana. It goes out entirely: that is the nidhana. This is the Rathantara sāman, woven into fire.
2.12.2: He who knows this Rathantara thus, woven into fire, gains the radiance of sacred learning and eats his food with a keen digestion, reaches the full span of life, lives brightly, becomes great in offspring and cattle, and great in fame. Facing the fire he should neither eat anything nor spit: that is his vow.
2.13.1: A man invites a woman: that is the hiṅkāra. He pleases her: that is the prastāva. He lies with the woman on one bed: that is the udgītha. He lies turned towards the woman: that is the pratihāra. He spends the time of union: that is the nidhana. He comes to its end: that is the nidhana. This is the Vāmadevya sāman, woven into the union of man and woman.
2.13.2: He who knows this Vāmadevya thus, woven into the union of man and woman, is never parted from a mate, has offspring from every union, reaches the full span of life, lives brightly, becomes great in offspring and cattle, and great in fame. He should not turn away any woman who comes to him seeking union: that is his vow.
2.14.1: The rising sun is the hiṅkāra, the risen sun the prastāva, midday the udgītha, the afternoon the pratihāra, and the setting sun the nidhana. This is the Bṛhat sāman, woven into the sun.
2.14.2: He who knows this Bṛhat thus, woven into the sun, becomes radiant and eats his food with a keen digestion, reaches the full span of life, lives brightly, becomes great in offspring and cattle, and great in fame. He should not speak ill of the sun as it burns: that is his vow.
2.15.1: Clouds gather: that is the hiṅkāra. A cloud forms: that is the prastāva. It rains: that is the udgītha. It flashes and thunders: that is the pratihāra. It holds back the rain: that is the nidhana. This is the Vairūpa sāman, woven into Parjanya, the god of rain.
2.15.2: He who knows this Vairūpa thus, woven into Parjanya, gains cattle of many forms and of fine form, reaches the full span of life, lives brightly, becomes great in offspring and cattle, and great in fame. He should not speak ill of the cloud as it rains: that is his vow.
2.16.1: Spring is the hiṅkāra, summer the prastāva, the rains the udgītha, autumn the pratihāra, winter the nidhana. This is the Vairāja sāman, woven into the seasons.
2.16.2: He who knows this Vairāja thus, woven into the seasons, shines with offspring, cattle and the radiance of sacred learning, reaches the full span of life, lives brightly, becomes great in offspring and cattle, and great in fame. He should not speak ill of the seasons: that is his vow.
2.17.1: The earth is the hiṅkāra, the mid-region the prastāva, the sky the udgītha, the quarters the pratihāra, and the ocean the nidhana. These are the Śakvarī sāmans, woven into the worlds.
2.17.2: He who knows these Śakvarīs thus, woven into the worlds, comes to possess the worlds, reaches the full span of life, lives brightly, becomes great in offspring and cattle, and great in fame. He should not speak ill of the worlds: that is his vow.
2.18.1: Goats are the hiṅkāra, sheep the prastāva, cows the udgītha, horses the pratihāra, man the nidhana. These are the Revatī sāmans, woven into the animals.
2.18.2: He who knows these Revatīs thus, woven into the animals, becomes rich in animals, reaches the full span of life, lives brightly, becomes great in offspring and cattle, and great in fame. He should not speak ill of animals: that is his vow.
2.19.1: Hair is the hiṅkāra, skin the prastāva, flesh the udgītha, bone the pratihāra, and marrow the nidhana. This is the Yajñāyajñīya sāman, woven into the limbs of the body.
2.19.2: He who knows this Yajñāyajñīya thus, woven into the limbs, becomes whole in his limbs and is crippled in none of them, reaches the full span of life, lives brightly, becomes great in offspring and cattle, and great in fame. He should not eat meat for a year: that is his vow. Or: he should never eat meat.
2.20.1: Agni, the fire, is the hiṅkāra; Vāyu, the wind, the prastāva; Āditya, the sun, the udgītha; the stars the pratihāra; and the moon the nidhana. This is the Rājana sāman, woven into the deities.
2.20.2: He who knows this Rājana thus, woven into the deities, attains the same world as these very deities, the same power as theirs, or union with them, reaches the full span of life, lives brightly, becomes great in offspring and cattle, and great in fame. He should not speak ill of brāhmaṇas: that is his vow.
2.21.1: The threefold knowledge, the three Vedas, is the hiṅkāra; these three worlds are the prastāva; Agni, Vāyu and Āditya are the udgītha; the stars, the birds and the rays of light are the pratihāra; the serpents, the gandharvas and the ancestors are the nidhana. This is the sāman woven into all.
2.21.2: He who knows this sāman thus, woven into all, becomes all.
2.21.3: On this there is a verse: Than those that are three and three in five ways, there is nothing else greater or higher.
2.21.4: He who knows that knows all; all the quarters bring him offerings. One should meditate thus: I am all. That is his vow, that is his vow.
2.22.1: I choose the sāman's vinardi chant, bellowing like a bull, which is good for cattle: such an udgītha belongs to Agni. The indistinct chant belongs to Prajāpati, the distinct to Soma, the soft and smooth to Vāyu, the smooth and forceful to Indra, the one like the cry of a curlew to Bṛhaspati, and the one that sounds like cracked bronze to Varuṇa. One should use all of these, but avoid only Varuṇa's.
2.22.2: Let me win immortality for the gods by my singing: with this thought one should sing. Svadhā, their offering, for the ancestors, the fulfilment of their hopes for men, grass and water for cattle, the heavenly world for the sacrificer, food for myself, let me win these by my singing: meditating on all these in his mind, he should sing the praise without a slip.
2.22.3: All the vowels are the selves of Indra, all the sibilants, the ūṣmans, the selves of Prajāpati, and all the stop consonants, the sparśas, the selves of Death. If anyone should find fault with him over the vowels, he should say to him: I had taken refuge in Indra; he will answer you.
2.22.4: And if anyone should find fault with him over the sibilants, he should say to him: I had taken refuge in Prajāpati; he will grind you to dust. And if anyone should find fault with him over the stops, he should say to him: I had taken refuge in Death; he will burn you to ashes.
2.22.5: All the vowels should be uttered resonant and strong, with the thought: let me give strength to Indra. All the sibilants should be uttered open, neither swallowed nor thrown out, with the thought: let me give myself over to Prajāpati. All the stops should be uttered gently, without running one into another, with the thought: let me withdraw myself from Death.
2.23.1: There are three branches of dharma, sacred duty. Sacrifice, study and giving are the first; austerity alone is the second; the brahmacārin, the student who lives in his teacher's house and wears his body down with its disciplines there for the rest of his life, is the third. All these gain worlds of merit; the one firmly established in Brahman, the absolute, attains immortality.
2.23.2: Prajāpati meditated with austerity upon the worlds. From the worlds so heated, the threefold knowledge flowed forth. He meditated with austerity upon it; from that knowledge so heated, these syllables flowed forth: bhūḥ, bhuvaḥ, svaḥ.
2.23.3: He meditated with austerity upon those syllables; from them, so heated, the syllable Om flowed forth. As all leaves are pierced through by their midrib, so all speech is pierced through by Om. Om is all this; Om is all this.
2.24.1: The expounders of Brahman say: The morning pressing of the soma belongs to the Vasus, the midday pressing to the Rudras, and the third pressing to the Ādityas and the Viśvedevas.
2.24.2: Where, then, is the world of the sacrificer? He who does not know it, how can he perform the sacrifice? Now, one who knows it should perform it.
2.24.3: Before the morning recitation (prātaranuvāka) begins, he, the sacrificer, sits down behind the Gārhapatya fire, facing north, and sings the sāman, the sacred chant, of the Vasus.
2.24.4: Open the door of the world; may we see you, for kingship (rājya).
2.24.5: Then he makes an offering, saying: Salutation to Agni, who dwells on the earth, who dwells in the world. Find a world for me, the sacrificer. This indeed is the sacrificer's world; I shall go to it.
2.24.6: To this world I, the sacrificer, shall go when my life is over. Svāhā. Strike away the bolt. Having said this, he rises. To him the Vasus hand over the morning savana, the first soma pressing of the day.
2.24.7: Before the midday savana begins, he sits down behind the Āgnīdhrīya fire, facing north, and sings the sāman of the Rudras.
2.24.8: Open the door of the world; may we see you, for wide sovereignty (vairājya).
2.24.9: Then he makes an offering, saying: Salutation to Vāyu, who dwells in the mid-region, who dwells in the world. Find a world for me, the sacrificer. This indeed is the sacrificer's world; I shall go to it.
2.24.10: To this world I, the sacrificer, shall go when my life is over. Svāhā. Strike away the bolt. Having said this, he rises. To him the Rudras hand over the midday savana.
2.24.11: Before the third savana begins, he sits down behind the Āhavanīya fire, facing north, and sings the sāman of the Ādityas and that of the Viśvedevas, the All-gods.
2.24.12: Open the door of the world; may we see you, for self-rule (svārājya).
2.24.13: That is the sāman of the Ādityas. Then that of the Viśvedevas: Open the door of the world; may we see you, for universal sovereignty (sāmrājya).
2.24.14: Then he makes an offering, saying: Salutation to the Ādityas and to the Viśvedevas, who dwell in heaven, who dwell in the world. Find a world for me, the sacrificer.
2.24.15: This indeed is the sacrificer's world; I shall go to it. To this world I, the sacrificer, shall go when my life is over. Svāhā. Strike away the bolt. Having said this, he rises.
2.24.16: To him the Ādityas and the Viśvedevas hand over the third savana. He indeed knows the true measure of the sacrifice, he who knows thus, he who knows thus.
3.1.1: That sun indeed is the honey of the gods. For this honey the sky is the cross-beam, the mid-region is the honeycomb, and the rays are the young bees.
3.1.2: Its rays that go to the east are its eastern honey-cells, the cells of the honeycomb. The ṛk verses are the bees, the Ṛgveda is the flower, and the waters of the offerings are the nectar. And these very ṛk verses —
3.1.3: These ṛk verses brooded over this Ṛgveda, and from it, so brooded over, there arose as its essence fame, lustre, vigour of the senses, strength and food to eat.
3.1.4: It flowed out, and went and settled at the side of the sun. That indeed is this red form of the sun.
3.2.1: Then, its rays that go to the south are its southern honey-cells. The yajus formulas are the bees, the Yajurveda is the flower, and the waters are the nectar.
3.2.2: Those very yajus formulas brooded over this Yajurveda, and from it, so brooded over, there arose as its essence fame, lustre, vigour of the senses, strength and food to eat.
3.2.3: It flowed out, and went and settled at the side of the sun. That indeed is this white form of the sun.
3.3.1: Then, its rays that go to the west are its western honey-cells. The sāman chants are the bees, the Sāmaveda is the flower, and the waters are the nectar.
3.3.2: Those very sāman chants brooded over this Sāmaveda, and from it, so brooded over, there arose as its essence fame, lustre, vigour of the senses, strength and food to eat.
3.3.3: It flowed out, and went and settled at the side of the sun. That indeed is this dark form of the sun.
3.4.1: Then, its rays that go to the north are its northern honey-cells. The Atharvāṅgiras hymns, those of the Atharvaveda, are the bees; the Itihāsa-Purāṇa, the ancient histories and lore, is the flower; and the waters are the nectar.
3.4.2: Those very Atharvāṅgiras hymns brooded over this Itihāsa-Purāṇa, and from it, so brooded over, there arose as its essence fame, lustre, vigour of the senses, strength and food to eat.
3.4.3: It flowed out, and went and settled at the side of the sun. That indeed is this intensely dark form of the sun.
3.5.1: Then, its rays that go upward are its upward honey-cells. The secret teachings are the bees, Brahman, here the syllable Om, is the flower, and the waters are the nectar.
3.5.2: Those very secret teachings brooded over this Brahman, and from it, so brooded over, there arose as its essence fame, lustre, vigour of the senses, strength and food to eat.
3.5.3: It flowed out, and went and settled at the side of the sun. That indeed is what seems to quiver in the middle of the sun.
3.5.4: These forms are the essences of the essences, for the Vedas are the essences, and these are their essences. They are the nectars of the nectars, for the Vedas are nectar, and these are their nectars.
3.6.1: Now, the first nectar (amṛta): the Vasus live on it, with Agni at their head. The gods indeed neither eat nor drink; they are satisfied just by seeing this very nectar.
3.6.2: They enter into this very form, and rise out of this form.
3.6.3: Whoever knows this nectar in this way becomes one of the Vasus, and with Agni at his head, is satisfied just by seeing this very nectar. He enters into this very form, and rises out of this form.
3.6.4: For as long as the sun goes on rising in the east and going down in the west, for that long he will attain to the lordship and self-rule of the Vasus.
3.7.1: Then, the second nectar: the Rudras live on it, with Indra at their head. The gods indeed neither eat nor drink; they are satisfied just by seeing this very nectar.
3.7.2: They enter into this very form, and rise out of this form.
3.7.3: Whoever knows this nectar in this way becomes one of the Rudras, and with Indra at his head, is satisfied just by seeing this very nectar. He enters into this very form, and rises out of this form.
3.7.4: For twice the time that the sun goes on rising in the east and going down in the west, it will rise in the south and go down in the north; for that long he will attain to the lordship and self-rule of the Rudras.
3.8.1: Then, the third nectar: the Ādityas live on it, with Varuṇa at their head. The gods indeed neither eat nor drink; they are satisfied just by seeing this very nectar.
3.8.2: They enter into this very form, and rise out of this form.
3.8.3: Whoever knows this nectar in this way becomes one of the Ādityas, and with Varuṇa at his head, is satisfied just by seeing this very nectar. He enters into this very form, and rises out of this form.
3.8.4: For twice the time that the sun goes on rising in the south and going down in the north, it will rise in the west and go down in the east; for that long he will attain to the lordship and self-rule of the Ādityas.
3.9.1: Then, the fourth nectar: the Maruts live on it, with Soma at their head. The gods indeed neither eat nor drink; they are satisfied just by seeing this very nectar.
3.9.2: They enter into this very form, and rise out of this form.
3.9.3: Whoever knows this nectar in this way becomes one of the Maruts, and with Soma at his head, is satisfied just by seeing this very nectar. He enters into this very form, and rises out of this form.
3.9.4: For twice the time that the sun goes on rising in the west and going down in the east, it will rise in the north and go down in the south; for that long he will attain to the lordship and self-rule of the Maruts.
3.10.1: Then, the fifth nectar: the Sādhyas live on it, with Brahmā at their head. The gods indeed neither eat nor drink; they are satisfied just by seeing this very nectar.
3.10.2: They enter into this very form, and rise out of this form.
3.10.3: Whoever knows this nectar in this way becomes one of the Sādhyas, and with Brahmā at his head, is satisfied just by seeing this very nectar. He enters into this very form, and rises out of this form.
3.10.4: For twice the time that the sun goes on rising in the north and going down in the south, it will rise above and go down below; for that long he will attain to the lordship and self-rule of the Sādhyas.
3.11.1: Then, having risen upward from there, the sun will rise no more and set no more; it will stand alone in the middle. On this there is this verse:
3.11.2: There, truly, it never set, nor did it ever rise. O gods, by this truth may I never be parted from Brahman, the supreme reality.
3.11.3: For him the sun truly neither rises nor sets; for him it is day, once and for all — for him who knows thus this secret teaching of Brahman.
3.11.4: Brahmā taught this to Prajāpati, Prajāpati to Manu, and Manu to his offspring. And this knowledge of Brahman was taught by his father to Uddālaka Āruṇi, his eldest son.
3.11.5: A father should impart this knowledge of Brahman only to his eldest son, or to a worthy disciple living with him.
3.11.6: To no one else at all, even if one were to give him this earth, girt by the waters and full of wealth; this alone is greater than that, this alone is greater than that.
3.12.1: The Gāyatrī truly is all this, every being there is. Speech truly is the Gāyatrī; it is speech that sings of all these beings and protects them.
3.12.2: That which is the Gāyatrī is truly this earth; for on it all beings rest, and they do not go beyond it.
3.12.3: That which is the earth is truly this body in a person; for in it these prāṇas, the vital breaths, rest, and they do not go beyond it.
3.12.4: That which is the body in a person is truly this heart within the person; for in it these prāṇas rest, and they do not go beyond it.
3.12.5: This Gāyatrī has four feet and is sixfold. This is declared also by a verse of the Ṛgveda:
3.12.6: Such is its greatness, and the Puruṣa is greater still. All beings are one foot of him; three feet of him are the immortal, in heaven.
3.12.7: That which is called Brahman is truly this space outside a person; and the space outside a person
3.12.8: That is truly this space within a person; and the space within a person
3.12.9: That is truly this space inside the heart. That is full and never moves away. He who knows thus gains a prosperity that is full and never moves away.
3.13.1: This heart has five openings of the gods. Its eastern opening is prāṇa; that is the eye, that is the sun. One should meditate on it as radiance and as food. He who knows thus becomes radiant and an eater of food.
3.13.2: And its southern opening is vyāna; that is the ear, that is the moon. One should meditate on it as prosperity and as fame. He who knows thus becomes prosperous and famous.
3.13.3: And its western opening is apāna; that is speech, that is fire. One should meditate on it as the lustre of sacred learning and as food. He who knows thus becomes lustrous with sacred learning and an eater of food.
3.13.4: And its northern opening is samāna; that is the mind, that is Parjanya, the god of rain. One should meditate on it as renown and beauty. He who knows thus becomes renowned and beautiful.
3.13.5: And its upper opening is udāna; that is the air, that is space. One should meditate on it as strength and greatness. He who knows thus becomes strong and great.
3.13.6: These, truly, are the five servants of Brahman, the doorkeepers of the heavenly world. One who knows thus these five servants of Brahman, the doorkeepers of the heavenly world — in his family a hero is born; he reaches the heavenly world, one who knows thus these five servants of Brahman, the doorkeepers of the heavenly world.
3.13.7: Now the light that shines beyond this heaven, above all, above everything, in the highest worlds, than which none are higher, is truly this light within a person.
3.13.8: This is how it is seen: when one feels by touch the warmth here in the body. This is how it is heard: when, closing the ears, one hears a sound like a rumble, like a bellow, like the roar of a blazing fire. One should meditate on it as seen and heard. He who knows thus becomes fair to look at and well known — he who knows thus.
3.14.1: All this truly is Brahman: from it all is born, into it all dissolves, in it all lives; so, being calm, one should meditate on it. For a person is made of resolve: as his resolve is in this world, so does he become on departing from here. So let him form a resolve.
3.14.2: He is made of mind; prāṇa is his body and light his form; his resolves are true, his self is like space; all works are his, all desires, all smells, all tastes; he pervades all this, without speech and without eagerness.
3.14.3: This ātman, my Self inside the heart, is smaller than a grain of rice, or a barleycorn, or a mustard seed, or a millet grain, or the kernel of a millet grain. This Self of mine inside the heart is vaster than the earth, vaster than the mid-region, vaster than heaven, vaster than these worlds.
3.14.4: All works are his, all desires, all smells, all tastes; he pervades all this, without speech and without eagerness: this is my Self inside the heart, this is Brahman. On departing from here I shall attain him. One who holds this as certain and has no doubt (attains it): so said Śāṇḍilya, so said Śāṇḍilya.
3.15.1: The chest whose belly is the mid-region and whose base is the earth does not decay. The quarters are its corners, and heaven is its opening above. This chest is a store of treasure; in it all this rests.
3.15.2: Its eastern quarter is named Juhū, the southern Sahamānā, the western Rājñī and the northern Subhūtā. The wind is the calf of these. He who knows this wind thus as the calf of the quarters does not weep for a son. I know this wind thus as the calf of the quarters; may I not weep for a son.
3.15.3: I go for refuge to the imperishable chest, with so-and-so, so-and-so, so-and-so. I go for refuge to prāṇa, with so-and-so, so-and-so, so-and-so. I go for refuge to bhūḥ, with so-and-so, so-and-so, so-and-so. I go for refuge to bhuvaḥ, with so-and-so, so-and-so, so-and-so. I go for refuge to svaḥ, with so-and-so, so-and-so, so-and-so.
3.15.4: When I said, I go for refuge to prāṇa — prāṇa truly is all this that exists, whatever there is; so it was to him that I went for refuge by those words.
3.15.5: And when I said, I go for refuge to bhūḥ, what I said was this: I go for refuge to the earth, I go for refuge to the mid-region, I go for refuge to heaven.
3.15.6: And when I said, I go for refuge to bhuvaḥ, what I said was this: I go for refuge to fire, I go for refuge to the wind, I go for refuge to the sun.
3.15.7: And when I said, I go for refuge to svaḥ, what I said was this: I go for refuge to the Ṛgveda, I go for refuge to the Yajurveda, I go for refuge to the Sāmaveda. That is what I said.
3.16.1: A man is indeed the sacrifice. His first twenty-four years are the morning pressing (of the soma); the Gāyatrī has twenty-four syllables, and the morning pressing belongs to the Gāyatrī. The Vasus are joined to that part of it. The prāṇas, the life-breaths, are indeed the Vasus, for they make all this dwell (in the body).
3.16.2: If in this period of life anything afflicts him, he should say: O prāṇas, O Vasus, carry this morning pressing of mine on into the midday pressing; let me, the sacrifice, not be cut off in the midst of the prāṇas, the Vasus. He rises up from it and becomes free of illness.
3.16.3: Then the forty-four years that follow are the midday pressing; the Triṣṭubh has forty-four syllables, and the midday pressing belongs to the Triṣṭubh. The Rudras are joined to that part of it. The prāṇas are indeed the Rudras, for they make all this weep.
3.16.4: If in this period of life anything afflicts him, he should say: O prāṇas, O Rudras, carry this midday pressing of mine on into the third pressing; let me, the sacrifice, not be cut off in the midst of the prāṇas, the Rudras. He rises up from it and becomes free of illness.
3.16.5: Then the forty-eight years that follow are the third pressing; the Jagatī has forty-eight syllables, and the third pressing belongs to the Jagatī. The Ādityas are joined to that part of it. The prāṇas are indeed the Ādityas, for they take all this in.
3.16.6: If in this period of life anything afflicts him, he should say: O prāṇas, O Ādityas, carry this third pressing of mine on to the full span of life; let me, the sacrifice, not be cut off in the midst of the prāṇas, the Ādityas. He rises up from it and becomes free of illness indeed.
3.16.7: Knowing this, Mahidāsa Aitareya, the son of Itarā, said: Why do you, illness, afflict me with this, when I shall not die of it? He lived a hundred and sixteen years. He who knows thus lives on to a hundred and sixteen years.
3.17.1: When he is hungry, when he is thirsty, when he finds no delight — these are his dīkṣās (the vows that open a sacrifice).
3.17.2: And when he eats, when he drinks, when he enjoys himself, that answers to the upasads (the days of the sacrifice kept on measured food).
3.17.3: And when he laughs, when he eats, when he has intercourse, that answers to the stutas and śastras alone (the praises that are sung and recited).
3.17.4: And austerity, giving, uprightness, non-violence and truthful speech — these are his dakṣiṇās (the gifts to the priests).
3.17.5: Therefore they say: soṣyati, she will give birth; asoṣṭa, she has given birth. That is indeed his being born again. Death is his avabhṛtha, the closing bath of the sacrifice.
3.17.6: Ghora Āṅgirasa taught this to Kṛṣṇa, the son of Devakī, and he became free of thirst for any other knowledge. Ghora Āṅgirasa said: At the hour of death one should repeat these three formulas: You are the imperishable; you are the unshaken; you are prāṇa, made fine and subtle. On this there are these two ṛks (Vedic verses).
3.17.7: Then (they see the light) of the ancient seed. Seeing the higher light beyond the darkness, seeing the higher light as our own, we have risen to Sūrya, god among the gods, the highest light — the highest light.
3.18.1: One should meditate on the mind as Brahman: this is with regard to the self. Now with regard to the gods: (one should meditate on) space as Brahman. Thus both are taught, with regard to the self and with regard to the gods.
3.18.2: That Brahman, the mind, has four quarters: speech is a quarter, prāṇa (the breath that smells) is a quarter, the eye is a quarter, the ear is a quarter — this is with regard to the self. Now with regard to the gods: fire is a quarter, air is a quarter, the sun is a quarter, the directions are a quarter. Thus both indeed are taught, with regard to the self and with regard to the gods.
3.18.3: Speech is indeed one of the four quarters of Brahman. It shines and glows with fire as its light. He who knows thus shines and glows with fame, renown and the radiance of sacred knowledge.
3.18.4: Prāṇa is indeed one of the four quarters of Brahman. It shines and glows with air as its light. He who knows thus shines and glows with fame, renown and the radiance of sacred knowledge.
3.18.5: The eye is indeed one of the four quarters of Brahman. It shines and glows with the sun as its light. He who knows thus shines and glows with fame, renown and the radiance of sacred knowledge.
3.18.6: The ear is indeed one of the four quarters of Brahman. It shines and glows with the directions as its light. He who knows thus shines and glows with fame, renown and the radiance of sacred knowledge — he who knows thus.
3.19.1: The teaching is: the sun is Brahman. Here is its explanation. In the beginning this was non-existent (unmanifest). It became existent. It grew. It turned into an egg. It lay for the span of a year. It broke open. The two halves of the eggshell became silver and gold.
3.19.2: Of these, the silver one is this earth; the gold one is the heaven. The outer membrane is the mountains; the inner membrane is the clouds and the mist; the veins are the rivers; the fluid in the bladder is the ocean.
3.19.3: And what was born from it is that sun. As it was being born, loud cries rose up after it, and all beings and all things desired. Therefore at its rising and at its going back (setting), loud cries rise up after it, and all beings and all things desired.
3.19.4: He who, knowing this so, meditates on the sun as Brahman — pleasing sounds will soon come to him and delight him, delight him.
4.1.1: There was Jānaśruti Pautrāyaṇa, who gave with faith, gave much, and had much food cooked (for guests). He had rest-houses built everywhere, thinking: Everywhere people will eat my food.
4.1.2: Then some swans flew past in the night. One swan said to another: Ho, ho, hey Bhallākṣa, Bhallākṣa! The light of Jānaśruti Pautrāyaṇa has spread out, equal to the sky. Do not touch it, lest it burn you.
4.1.3: The other replied to him: Hey, who is he, such as he is, that you speak of him as if he were Raikva with the cart? The first swan asked: What is he like, this Raikva with the cart?
4.1.4: The other swan said: As all the lower throws go to the kṛta, the highest throw at dice, when it wins, so all the good that people do comes to him. And whoever knows what he knows, he too is the one I have spoken of thus.
4.1.5: Jānaśruti Pautrāyaṇa overheard this. Even as he was rising, he said to his attendant: My dear, do you speak of me as if I were Raikva with the cart? The attendant asked: What is he like, this Raikva with the cart?
4.1.6: Jānaśruti said: As all the lower throws go to the kṛta, the highest throw at dice, when it wins, so all the good that people do comes to him. And whoever knows what he knows, he too is the one I have spoken of thus.
4.1.7: The attendant searched, and came back saying: I did not find him. Jānaśruti said to him: Hey, look for him where one looks for a brāhmaṇa (a knower of Brahman).
4.1.8: He sat down near a man who was scratching his itch under a cart, and asked him: Revered sir, are you Raikva with the cart? He acknowledged it: Yes, I am, hey. The attendant came back, saying: I have found him.
4.2.1: Then Jānaśruti Pautrāyaṇa took six hundred cows, a gold necklace and a chariot with a team of she-mules, went to him and said to him:
4.2.2: Raikva, here are six hundred cows, this necklace, this chariot with its team of she-mules. Revered sir, teach me that deity, the deity you meditate on.
4.2.3: Raikva replied to him: Let the necklace and the chariot stay with you, śūdra, along with the cows. Then Jānaśruti Pautrāyaṇa took a thousand cows, a gold necklace, a chariot with a team of she-mules and his daughter, and went to him again.
4.2.4: Jānaśruti said to him: Raikva, here are a thousand cows, this necklace, this chariot with its team of she-mules, this wife, and this village in which you live. Revered sir, do teach me.
4.2.5: Taking her face as the door to the teaching, Raikva said: You have brought these, śūdra; by this face (this means) alone you will make me speak. Those villages in the Mahāvṛṣa country where he lived, given to him (by the king), are named Raikvaparṇa. Then Raikva said to him:
4.3.1: Air is indeed the gatherer (saṃvarga, which takes all into itself). When fire goes out, it goes into air alone; when the sun sets, it goes into air alone; when the moon sets, it goes into air alone.
4.3.2: When the waters dry up, they go into air alone, for air gathers all these into itself. This is with regard to the gods.
4.3.3: Now with regard to the self: prāṇa is indeed the gatherer. When a man sleeps, speech goes into prāṇa alone, the eye into prāṇa, the ear into prāṇa, the mind into prāṇa; for prāṇa gathers all these into itself.
4.3.4: These, then, are the two gatherers: air among the gods, prāṇa among the senses (the prāṇas).
4.3.5: Once, as Śaunaka Kāpeya and Abhipratārin Kākṣaseni were being served their meal, a brahmacārin (a student of the Veda) begged food of them. They did not give him any.
4.3.6: The brahmacārin said: One god, Ka (Prajāpati), the guardian of the world, swallowed four great ones. O Kāpeya, mortals do not see him, O Abhipratārin, though he dwells in many forms. He to whom this food belongs — to him it has not been given.
4.3.7: Śaunaka Kāpeya, thinking it over, came to him and said: He is the Self of the gods, the begetter of creatures, golden-toothed, the devourer, the wise; they call his greatness great, for, himself uneaten, he eats even what is not food. This, O brahmacārin, is what we meditate on. Give him alms.
4.3.8: They gave to him. These five and those other five, being ten, make the kṛta (the highest throw at dice). Therefore in all the directions the ten are food, the kṛta. This is Virāj, the eater of food; by it all this is seen. All this comes to be seen by him, and he becomes an eater of food, who knows thus — who knows thus.
4.4.1: Satyakāma Jābāla addressed his mother Jabālā: Revered mother, I shall live as a brahmacārin, a student staying with a teacher. Of what lineage (gotra) am I?
4.4.2: She said to him: My son, I do not know of what lineage you are. In my youth I was a serving woman, going about many tasks, and then I had you; so I do not know of what lineage you are. I am Jabālā by name, and you are Satyakāma by name; so call yourself just Satyakāma Jābāla.
4.4.3: He went to Hāridrumata Gautama and said: I shall live as a brahmacārin with your reverence; may I come to you (as a pupil)?
4.4.4: Gautama asked him: Dear one, of what lineage are you? He said: Sir, I do not know of what lineage I am. I asked my mother, and she answered me: In my youth I was a serving woman, going about many tasks, and then I had you; so I do not know of what lineage you are. I am Jabālā by name, and you are Satyakāma by name. So I am Satyakāma Jābāla, sir.
4.4.5: Gautama said to him: No one but a brāhmaṇa could speak out so plainly. Fetch the fuel, dear one; I shall initiate you, for you have not swerved from the truth. Having initiated him, he set apart four hundred lean and weak cows and said: Follow these, dear one. As Satyakāma drove them off, he said: I shall not come back until they are a thousand. He lived away for a number of years, till the cows had grown to a thousand.
4.5.1: Then a bull spoke to him: Satyakāma! He answered: Revered sir! The bull said: Dear one, we have reached a thousand; take us to the teacher's house.
4.5.2: And let me tell you a quarter of Brahman, the supreme reality. Satyakāma said: Let the revered one tell me. The bull told him: The east is a part, the west is a part, the south is a part, the north is a part. This, dear one, is the quarter of Brahman made of four parts, and its name is Prakāśavān, the Shining.
4.5.3: Whoever, knowing it so, meditates on this four-part quarter of Brahman as the Shining, becomes shining in this world and wins worlds that are shining: whoever, knowing it so, meditates on this four-part quarter of Brahman as the Shining.
4.6.1: The bull said: Agni, the fire, will tell you a quarter. The next day he drove the cows on. Where evening found them, there he kindled a fire, penned the cows in, laid fuel on the fire and sat down west of it, facing east.
4.6.2: Agni called to him: Satyakāma! He answered: Revered sir!
4.6.3: Dear one, let me tell you a quarter of Brahman. Satyakāma said: Let the revered one tell me. Agni told him: The earth is a part, the mid-air is a part, the sky is a part, the ocean is a part. This, dear one, is the quarter of Brahman made of four parts, and its name is Anantavān, the Endless.
4.6.4: Whoever, knowing it so, meditates on this four-part quarter of Brahman as the Endless, becomes endless in this world and wins worlds that are endless: whoever, knowing it so, meditates on this four-part quarter of Brahman as the Endless.
4.7.1: Agni said: A swan will tell you a quarter. The next day he drove the cows on. Where evening found them, there he kindled a fire, penned the cows in, laid fuel on the fire and sat down west of it, facing east.
4.7.2: The swan flew down beside him and called: Satyakāma! He answered: Revered sir!
4.7.3: Dear one, let me tell you a quarter of Brahman. Satyakāma said: Let the revered one tell me. The swan told him: Fire is a part, the sun is a part, the moon is a part, lightning is a part. This, dear one, is the quarter of Brahman made of four parts, and its name is Jyotiṣmān, the Luminous.
4.7.4: Whoever, knowing it so, meditates on this four-part quarter of Brahman as the Luminous, becomes luminous in this world and wins worlds that are luminous: whoever, knowing it so, meditates on this four-part quarter of Brahman as the Luminous.
4.8.1: The swan said: A diver-bird will tell you a quarter. The next day he drove the cows on. Where evening found them, there he kindled a fire, penned the cows in, laid fuel on the fire and sat down west of it, facing east.
4.8.2: The diver-bird flew down beside him and called: Satyakāma! He answered: Revered sir!
4.8.3: Dear one, let me tell you a quarter of Brahman. Satyakāma said: Let the revered one tell me. The diver-bird told him: Prāṇa, the breath, is a part, the eye is a part, the ear is a part, the mind is a part. This, dear one, is the quarter of Brahman made of four parts, and its name is Āyatanavān, the one with an abode.
4.8.4: Whoever, knowing it so, meditates on this four-part quarter of Brahman as the one with an abode, comes to have an abode in this world and wins worlds that have abodes: whoever, knowing it so, meditates on this four-part quarter of Brahman as the one with an abode.
4.9.1: He reached the teacher's house. The teacher called to him: Satyakāma! He answered: Revered sir!
4.9.2: The teacher said: Dear one, you shine like one who knows Brahman. Who has taught you? He owned: Beings other than men. But I wish that you yourself, revered sir, would teach me.
4.9.3: For I have heard from men like your reverence that only knowledge learned from a teacher comes to its best. Then the teacher taught him that same knowledge; nothing in it was left out, nothing was left out.
4.10.1: Upakosala Kāmalāyana lived as a brahmacārin with Satyakāma Jābāla. For twelve years he tended his teacher's fires. Satyakāma let his other pupils go home, but him alone he did not let go.
4.10.2: His wife said to him: The student has done his austerities and tended the fires well. Do not let the fires reproach you; teach him. But he went away on a journey without teaching him anything.
4.10.3: Out of grief, Upakosala resolved to fast. The teacher's wife said to him: Student, eat. Why do you not eat? He said: Many are the desires in this man, running many ways; I am full of ailments. I will not eat.
4.10.4: Then the fires said to one another: The student has done his austerities and tended us well; come, let us teach him. They said to him: Prāṇa is Brahman, ka (joy) is Brahman, kha (space) is Brahman.
4.10.5: He said: I understand that prāṇa is Brahman, but ka and kha I do not understand. They said: What is ka is the same as kha; what is kha is the same as ka. And they taught him of prāṇa and of the space that is its seat.
4.11.1: Then the Gārhapatya, the householder's fire, taught him: The earth, fire, food and the sun (are my four forms). The person who is seen in the sun: I am he; he indeed am I.
4.11.2: Whoever, knowing it so, meditates on it destroys his sinful deeds, comes to possess a world (ours), reaches the full span of life and lives brightly; his descendants do not die out. We protect him in this world and in the next: whoever, knowing it so, meditates on it.
4.12.1: Then the Anvāhāryapacana, the southern fire, taught him: Water, the quarters, the stars and the moon (are my four forms). The person who is seen in the moon: I am he; he indeed am I.
4.12.2: Whoever, knowing it so, meditates on it destroys his sinful deeds, comes to possess a world (ours), reaches the full span of life and lives brightly; his descendants do not die out. We protect him in this world and in the next: whoever, knowing it so, meditates on it.
4.13.1: Then the Āhavanīya, the fire of offerings, taught him: Prāṇa, space, the sky and lightning (are my four forms). The person who is seen in lightning: I am he; he indeed am I.
4.13.2: Whoever, knowing it so, meditates on it destroys his sinful deeds, comes to possess a world (ours), reaches the full span of life and lives brightly; his descendants do not die out. We protect him in this world and in the next: whoever, knowing it so, meditates on it.
4.14.1: The fires said: Upakosala, dear one, this is our knowledge for you, and the knowledge of the Self; but your teacher will tell you the way. Then his teacher came back. The teacher called to him: Upakosala!
4.14.2: He answered: Revered sir! The teacher said: Dear one, your face shines like that of one who knows Brahman. Who has taught you? Upakosala said: Who would teach me, sir? So he half hid it, and pointing to the fires he said: These, surely, look like this now; before, they were otherwise. The teacher asked: Dear one, what did they tell you?
4.14.3: He owned: This. The teacher said: Dear one, they spoke to you only of the worlds; but I shall tell you that, Brahman. As water does not cling to a lotus leaf, so no evil deed clings to one who knows it so. Upakosala said: Let the revered one tell me. The teacher said to him:
4.15.1: The person who is seen in the eye is the Self, he said. This is the immortal, the fearless; this is Brahman. Even if ghee or water is poured there, into the eye, it runs off to the lids alone.
4.15.2: They call him Saṃyadvāma, for all lovely things come together in him. All lovely things come together in whoever knows thus.
4.15.3: He is also Vāmanī, for he brings all lovely things. Whoever knows thus brings all lovely things.
4.15.4: He is also Bhāmanī, for he shines in all the worlds. Whoever knows thus shines in all the worlds.
4.15.5: Now, whether or not the funeral rites are done for such a one, they pass into the flame; from the flame into the day; from the day into the bright fortnight; from the bright fortnight into the six months in which the sun moves north; from those months into the year; from the year into the sun; from the sun into the moon; from the moon into lightning. There a person not human leads them to Brahman. This is the path of the gods, the path to Brahman. Those who go by it do not return to this human whirl; they do not return.
4.16.1: This that blows, the wind, is truly the sacrifice. As it moves, it purifies all this; and because as it moves it purifies all this, it alone is the sacrifice. Mind and speech are its two tracks.
4.16.2: Of these, the brahmā, the priest who oversees the sacrifice, shapes one with the mind, and the hotṛ, the adhvaryu and the udgātṛ shape the other with speech. Now if, after the morning litany has begun and before the closing verse, the brahmā breaks his silence,
4.16.3: then he shapes only one track, and the other is lost. As a one-legged man who walks, or a chariot running on one wheel, comes to harm, so his sacrifice comes to harm; and as the sacrifice comes to harm, the sacrificer comes to harm with it. Having sacrificed, he is the worse for it.
4.16.4: But if, after the morning litany has begun, the brahmā does not break his silence before the closing verse, they shape both tracks, and neither is lost.
4.16.5: As a man who walks on both legs, or a chariot running on both wheels, stands firm, so his sacrifice stands firm; and as the sacrifice stands firm, the sacrificer stands firm with it. Having sacrificed, he is the better for it.
4.17.1: Prajāpati brooded over the worlds. From them, as they were brooded over, he drew out their essences: fire from the earth, the wind from the mid-air and the sun from the sky.
4.17.2: He brooded over these three deities. From them, as they were brooded over, he drew out their essences: the ṛk verses from fire, the yajus formulas from the wind and the sāman chants from the sun.
4.17.3: He brooded over this threefold knowledge, the three Vedas. From it, as it was brooded over, he drew out its essences: bhūḥ from the ṛks, bhuvaḥ from the yajuses and svaḥ from the sāmans.
4.17.4: So if the sacrifice is harmed on the side of the ṛks, he should offer into the gārhapatya fire, saying bhūḥ svāhā. In this way, by the essence of the ṛks themselves, by the power of the ṛks, he mends the breach in the ṛk part of the sacrifice.
4.17.5: And if it is harmed on the side of the yajuses, he should offer into the dakṣiṇāgni, the southern fire, saying bhuvaḥ svāhā. In this way, by the essence of the yajuses themselves, by the power of the yajuses, he mends the breach in the yajus part of the sacrifice.
4.17.6: And if it is harmed on the side of the sāmans, he should offer into the āhavanīya fire, saying svaḥ svāhā. In this way, by the essence of the sāmans themselves, by the power of the sāmans, he mends the breach in the sāman part of the sacrifice.
4.17.7: As one would join gold with salt (borax), silver with gold, tin with silver, lead with tin, iron with lead, wood with iron, and wood with leather,
4.17.8: so, by the power of these worlds, of these deities and of this threefold knowledge, he mends the breach in the sacrifice. A sacrifice in which the brahmā knows this is truly one that has been given its medicine.
4.17.9: A sacrifice in which the brahmā knows this truly slopes towards the north, towards the northern path. Of the brahmā who knows this there is this verse: Wherever the sacrifice turns back, there he goes.
4.17.10: The brahmā, the silent one, is the one priest who guards the Kurus, the performers of the sacrifice, as a mare guards her riders. The brahmā who knows this guards the sacrifice, the sacrificer and all the priests. Therefore one should make only one who knows this the brahmā, never one who does not, never one who does not.
5.1.1: One who knows the eldest and the best becomes the eldest and the best. Prāṇa, the breath of life, is indeed the eldest and the best.
5.1.2: One who knows the richest becomes the richest among his own people. Speech is indeed the richest.
5.1.3: One who knows the firm ground stands firm in this world and in the next. The eye is indeed the firm ground.
5.1.4: One who knows fulfilment has his desires fulfilled, both divine and human. The ear is indeed fulfilment.
5.1.5: One who knows the abode becomes the abode of his own people. The mind is indeed the abode.
5.1.6: Once the prāṇas, the powers of life in the body, quarrelled over which was the best: I am the best, I am the best.
5.1.7: The prāṇas went to Prajāpati, their father, and said: Revered sir, which of us is the best? He said to them: The one of you on whose going out the body looks the most wretched, that one is the best of you.
5.1.8: Speech went out. After staying away a year, it came back and said: How were you able to live without me? The others said: As the mute live, not speaking but breathing with the breath, seeing with the eye, hearing with the ear and thinking with the mind, so we lived. Then speech entered again.
5.1.9: The eye went out. After staying away a year, it came back and said: How were you able to live without me? The others said: As the blind live, not seeing but breathing with the breath, speaking with speech, hearing with the ear and thinking with the mind, so we lived. Then the eye entered again.
5.1.10: The ear went out. After staying away a year, it came back and said: How were you able to live without me? The others said: As the deaf live, not hearing but breathing with the breath, speaking with speech, seeing with the eye and thinking with the mind, so we lived. Then the ear entered again.
5.1.11: The mind went out. After staying away a year, it came back and said: How were you able to live without me? The others said: As infants live without a mind, but breathing with the breath, speaking with speech, seeing with the eye and hearing with the ear, so we lived. Then the mind entered again.
5.1.12: Then prāṇa was about to go out, and as a fine horse would tear up the pegs that tether its feet, so it tore up the other prāṇas. They all came to it together and said: Revered sir, be our master; you are the best of us; do not go out.
5.1.13: Then speech said to it: In that I am the richest, it is you who are the richest. Then the eye said to it: In that I am the firm ground, it is you who are the firm ground.
5.1.14: Then the ear said to it: In that I am fulfilment, it is you who are fulfilment. Then the mind said to it: In that I am the abode, it is you who are the abode.
5.1.15: People do not call them speeches, eyes, ears or minds; they call them prāṇas, for it is prāṇa that is all these.
5.2.1: Prāṇa said: What will be my food? Speech and the others said: Whatever there is here, down to dogs and birds. All this is the food of ana; ana is the direct name of prāṇa. For one who knows this, there is nothing that is not food.
5.2.2: Prāṇa said: What will be my clothing? They said: Water. That is why people about to eat clothe prāṇa with water before the meal and after it. One who knows this obtains clothing and is never naked.
5.2.3: Satyakāma Jābāla, having taught this to Gośruti Vaiyāghrapadya, said: Even if one were to tell this to a dry stump, branches would grow on it and leaves would sprout.
5.2.4: Now if one wishes to attain greatness, he should take the vow of dīkṣā on the new-moon day; then, on the night of the full moon, having stirred a mash of all herbs in curd and honey, he should offer ghee into the fire with svāhā to the eldest and best, and pour the remaining drops into the mash.
5.2.5: He should offer ghee into the fire with svāhā to the richest, and pour the remaining drops into the mash; offer ghee into the fire with svāhā to the firm ground, and pour the remaining drops into the mash; offer ghee into the fire with svāhā to fulfilment, and pour the remaining drops into the mash; offer ghee into the fire with svāhā to the abode, and pour the remaining drops into the mash.
5.2.6: Then, stepping back a little from the fire and holding the mash in his cupped hands, he mutters: You are Ama by name, for all this is together (amā) with you. He is the eldest and the best, the king, the overlord. May he bring me to eldership, to being the best, to kingship and to overlordship. May I become all this.
5.2.7: Then he eats it quarter by quarter with this ṛk: with tat savitur vṛṇīmahe (we choose that of Savitṛ) he takes a mouthful; with vayaṃ devasya bhojanam (we … the food of the god) he takes a mouthful; with śreṣṭhaṃ sarvadhātamam (the best, the all-sustaining) he takes a mouthful; with turaṃ bhagasya dhīmahi (may we swiftly meditate on Bhaga's form) he drinks it all. Having washed the bowl or cup (kaṃsa or camasa), he lies down behind the fire, on a skin or on the bare ground, silent and not overcome by anything. If in a dream he sees a woman, he should know that his rite has prospered.
