5.2.8: On this there is a verse: When, in rites done for a desire, people see a woman in their dreams, one should know success in it from that sight in a dream, from that sight in a dream.
5.3.1: Śvetaketu, the son of Āruṇi, came to the assembly of the Pañcālas. Pravāhaṇa Jaivali said to him: Boy, has your father taught you? He said: Yes, revered sir, he has.
5.3.2: Pravāhaṇa asked: Do you know where beings go upward from here? No, revered sir. Do you know in what way they come back? No, revered sir. Do you know where the two paths part, the path of the gods (devayāna) and the path of the fathers (pitṛyāṇa)? No, revered sir.
5.3.3: Do you know how it is that that world is never filled up? No, revered sir. Do you know how, at the fifth offering, water comes to be called man? Not at all, revered sir.
5.3.4: Then why did you tell me you were taught? How could a man who does not know these things claim to have been taught? Distressed by this, he went to his father's place and said to him: Revered sir, without teaching me you told me: I have taught you.
5.3.5: That so-called kṣatriya asked me five questions, and I could not explain even one of them. His father said: As you have just told them to me, so it is with me: I do not know even one of them. Had I known them, how could I not have told you?
5.3.6: Gautama went to the king's place. When he arrived, the king paid him due honour. In the morning, when the king was in the assembly, Gautama went up to him. The king said to him: Revered Gautama, choose a boon of human wealth. He said: Let human wealth stay with you, O king. Tell me the very words you spoke in the boy's presence. The king was troubled.
5.3.7: He bade him: Stay here a long while. Then he said to him: Gautama, as you have spoken to me, so hear: before you, this knowledge never went to brāhmaṇas; that is why in all the worlds its teaching belonged to the kṣatriya alone. Then he told him.
5.4.1: That world yonder, O Gautama, is indeed a fire. The sun itself is its fuel, the rays its smoke, the day its flame, the moon its embers, and the stars its sparks.
5.4.2: In this very fire the gods offer faith. From that offering King Soma arises.
5.5.1: Parjanya, the god of rain, O Gautama, is indeed a fire. The air itself is its fuel, the cloud its smoke, the lightning its flame, the thunderbolt its embers, and the rumblings of thunder its sparks.
5.5.2: In this very fire the gods offer King Soma. From that offering rain arises.
5.6.1: The earth, O Gautama, is indeed a fire. The year itself is its fuel, space its smoke, the night its flame, the quarters its embers, and the intermediate quarters its sparks.
5.6.2: In this very fire the gods offer rain. From that offering food arises.
5.7.1: Man, O Gautama, is indeed a fire. Speech itself is its fuel, prāṇa, the breath, its smoke, the tongue its flame, the eye its embers, and the ear its sparks.
5.7.2: In this very fire the gods offer food. From that offering semen arises.
5.8.1: Woman, O Gautama, is indeed a fire. Her generative organ itself is its fuel; his calling her to him is its smoke; the womb its flame; what is done within, its embers; and the delights, its sparks.
5.8.2: In this very fire the gods offer semen. From that offering the foetus arises.
5.9.1: In this way, in the fifth offering, the waters come to bear the name of man. Covered by its membrane, that foetus lies within for ten months or nine, or for however long, and then is born.
5.9.2: Once born, he lives as long as his span of life lasts. When he has died and gone where his deeds direct, they carry him from here to the fire itself, from which he came, from which he arose.
5.10.1: Of these, those who know this thus, and those who in the forest worship faith and austerity, pass into the flame; out of the flame into the day; out of the day into the fortnight of the waxing moon; out of the waxing fortnight into the six months when the sun travels north.
5.10.2: Out of those months into the year; out of the year into the sun; out of the sun into the moon; out of the moon into the lightning. There is a being who is not human; he leads them to Brahman. This is the path of the gods.
5.10.3: But those who here in the village worship sacrifices, works of public good and gifts pass into the smoke; out of the smoke into the night; out of the night into the fortnight of the waning moon; out of the waning fortnight into the six months when the sun travels south. These do not reach the year.
5.10.4: Out of those months into the world of the fathers; out of the world of the fathers into space; out of space into the moon. That is King Soma; that is the food of the gods; the gods eat it.
5.10.5: Having dwelt there until their deeds are spent, they return by that same path, just as they went: to space, and from space to the air. Having become air, one becomes smoke; having become smoke, one becomes cloud.
5.10.6: Having become cloud, one becomes rain-cloud; having become rain-cloud, one rains down. Here they are born as rice and barley, herbs and trees, sesame and beans. From this, escape is harder still; for it is in the likeness of whoever eats that food and pours out the seed that one comes to be again.
5.10.7: Of these, those whose conduct here has been pleasing will soon enter a pleasing womb: the womb of a brāhmaṇa, of a kṣatriya or of a vaiśya. But those whose conduct here has been foul will soon enter a foul womb: the womb of a dog, of a pig or of a caṇḍāla, one born outside the four classes.
5.10.8: But those who go by neither of these two paths become these small creatures that come back time after time. Be born and die: that is the third state. Because of it, that world yonder is never filled. Therefore one should shrink from it. On this there is this verse:
5.10.9: The thief of gold, the drinker of liquor, the one who lies in his teacher's bed, and the killer of a brāhmaṇa: these four fall, and the fifth too, who keeps company with them.
5.10.10: But he who knows these five fires thus is not stained by sin even when he keeps company with them. He becomes pure and cleansed, and a holy world is his, he who knows thus, he who knows thus.
5.11.1: Prācīnaśāla Aupamanyava, Satyayajña Pauluṣi, Indradyumna Bhāllaveya, Jana Śārkarākṣya and Buḍila Āśvatarāśvi, great householders and great Vedic scholars, came together and deliberated: What is our ātman, our Self? What is Brahman?
5.11.2: They agreed: Revered sirs, this Uddālaka Āruṇi knows well this Vaiśvānara Self, the universal Self. Come, let us go to him. And they went to him.
5.11.3: Uddālaka reflected: These great householders and great Vedic scholars will question me, and I shall not be able to answer them in full. Well then, let me direct them to another.
5.11.4: Uddālaka said to them: Revered sirs, this Aśvapati Kaikeya knows well this Vaiśvānara Self. Come, let us go to him. And they went to him.
5.11.5: When they arrived, the king had honours paid to each of them separately. Rising in the morning, he said: My kingdom has no thief, no miser, no drinker of liquor, no one who has not set up the sacred fires, no one unlearned, no man who follows his lust; how then a woman who follows hers? Revered sirs, I am about to perform a sacrifice. As much wealth as I give to each priest, so much shall I give to you, sirs. Stay, sirs.
5.11.6: They said: The purpose for which a man comes is the very thing he should speak of. You know well this Vaiśvānara Self; tell us of that.
5.11.7: The king said to them: In the morning I shall give you an answer. In the forenoon they came back to him, fuel in hand. Without first initiating them, he said this to them:
5.12.1: The king asked: Aupamanyava, whom do you worship as the Self? He answered: Heaven alone, revered king. The king said: This is the Vaiśvānara Self called Sutejas, the brightly shining, which you worship as the Self; therefore in your family soma is seen pressed, pressed forth and pressed in abundance.
5.12.2: You eat food and see what is dear. Whoever worships this Vaiśvānara Self thus eats food and sees what is dear, and in his family there is the splendour of sacred learning. But this is only the head of the Self, the king said; your head would have fallen off had you not come to me.
5.13.1: Then the king addressed Satyayajña Pauluṣi: Prācīnayogya, whom do you worship as the Self? He answered: The sun alone, revered king. The king said: This is the Vaiśvānara Self called Viśvarūpa, of every form, which you worship as the Self; therefore abundance of every kind is seen in your family.
5.13.2: At your service are a chariot drawn by she-mules and maidservants with a gold necklace. You eat food and see what is dear. Whoever worships this Vaiśvānara Self thus eats food and sees what is dear, and in his family there is the splendour of sacred learning. But this is only the eye of the Self, the king said; you would have gone blind had you not come to me.
5.14.1: Then the king addressed Indradyumna Bhāllaveya: Vaiyāghrapadya, whom do you worship as the Self? He answered: The air alone, revered king. The king said: This is the Vaiśvānara Self called Pṛthagvartman, of many courses, which you worship as the Self; therefore tributes come to you from many sides, and rows of chariots follow you from many sides.
5.14.2: You eat food and see what is dear. Whoever worships this Vaiśvānara Self thus eats food and sees what is dear, and in his family there is the splendour of sacred learning. But this is only the prāṇa of the Self, the king said; your prāṇa would have left you had you not come to me.
5.15.1: Then the king addressed Jana: Śārkarākṣya, whom do you worship as the Self? He answered: Space alone, revered king. The king said: This is the Vaiśvānara Self called Bahula, the abundant, which you worship as the Self; therefore you are abundant in offspring and in wealth.
5.15.2: You eat food and see what is dear. Whoever worships this Vaiśvānara Self thus eats food and sees what is dear, and in his family there is the splendour of sacred learning. But this is only the trunk of the Self, the king said; your trunk would have wasted away had you not come to me.
5.16.1: Then the king addressed Buḍila Āśvatarāśvi: Vaiyāghrapadya, whom do you worship as the Self? He answered: The waters alone, revered king. The king said: This is the Vaiśvānara Self called Rayi, wealth, which you worship as the Self; therefore you are wealthy and well nourished.
5.16.2: You eat food and see what is dear. Whoever worships this Vaiśvānara Self thus eats food and sees what is dear, and in his family there is the splendour of sacred learning. But this is only the bladder of the Self, the king said; your bladder would have burst had you not come to me.
5.17.1: Then the king addressed Uddālaka Āruṇi: Gautama, whom do you worship as the Self? He answered: The earth alone, revered king. The king said: This is the Vaiśvānara Self called Pratiṣṭhā, the foundation, which you worship as the Self; therefore you are firmly established in offspring and in cattle.
5.17.2: You eat food and see what is dear. Whoever worships this Vaiśvānara Self thus eats food and sees what is dear, and in his family there is the splendour of sacred learning. But these are only the feet of the Self, the king said; your feet would have withered had you not come to me.
5.18.1: Aśvapati said to them: You eat food knowing this Self, Vaiśvānara, as though it were separate parts. But one who worships this Self, Vaiśvānara, thus, as measured by the regions from heaven to earth and known within as one's own Self, eats food in all worlds, in all beings and in all selves.
5.18.2: Of this Self, Vaiśvānara, the head is Sutejas, heaven; the eye is Viśvarūpa, the sun; the breath is Pṛthagvartman, the air; the trunk is Bahula, space; the bladder is Rayi, water; and the feet are the earth itself. The chest is the altar, the hairs are the sacred grass, the heart is the gārhapatya, the householder's fire, the mind is the anvāhāryapacana, the southern fire, and the mouth is the āhavanīya, the fire of offering.
5.19.1: So the food that comes first at a meal is fit to be offered. The first oblation the eater makes he should make saying: prāṇāya svāhā. Then prāṇa, the breath, is satisfied.
5.19.2: When prāṇa is satisfied, the eye is satisfied; when the eye is satisfied, the sun is satisfied; when the sun is satisfied, heaven is satisfied; when heaven is satisfied, whatever heaven and the sun preside over is satisfied. Following that satisfaction, the one who eats is himself satisfied with offspring, cattle, food to eat, radiance and the radiance of sacred learning.
5.20.1: Then the second oblation he makes he should make saying: vyānāya svāhā. Then vyāna is satisfied.
5.20.2: When vyāna is satisfied, the ear is satisfied; when the ear is satisfied, the moon is satisfied; when the moon is satisfied, the quarters are satisfied; when the quarters are satisfied, whatever the quarters and the moon preside over is satisfied. Following that satisfaction, the one who eats is himself satisfied with offspring, cattle, food to eat, radiance and the radiance of sacred learning.
5.21.1: Then the third oblation he makes he should make saying: apānāya svāhā. Then apāna is satisfied.
5.21.2: When apāna is satisfied, speech is satisfied; when speech is satisfied, fire is satisfied; when fire is satisfied, the earth is satisfied; when the earth is satisfied, whatever the earth and fire preside over is satisfied. Following that satisfaction, the one who eats is himself satisfied with offspring, cattle, food to eat, radiance and the radiance of sacred learning.
5.22.1: Then the fourth oblation he makes he should make saying: samānāya svāhā. Then samāna is satisfied.
5.22.2: When samāna is satisfied, the mind is satisfied; when the mind is satisfied, the rain-cloud is satisfied; when the rain-cloud is satisfied, lightning is satisfied; when lightning is satisfied, whatever lightning and the rain-cloud preside over is satisfied. Following that satisfaction, the one who eats is himself satisfied with offspring, cattle, food to eat, radiance and the radiance of sacred learning.
5.23.1: Then the fifth oblation he makes he should make saying: udānāya svāhā. Then udāna is satisfied.
5.23.2: When udāna is satisfied, the skin is satisfied; when the skin is satisfied, the wind is satisfied; when the wind is satisfied, space is satisfied; when space is satisfied, whatever the wind and space preside over is satisfied. Following that satisfaction, the one who eats is himself satisfied with offspring, cattle, food to eat, radiance and the radiance of sacred learning.
5.24.1: One who offers the Agnihotra without knowing this, his offering would be like pushing aside the live coals and pouring the oblation on the ashes.
5.24.2: But one who offers the Agnihotra knowing this thus, his offering is made in all worlds, in all beings and in all selves.
5.24.3: As the fluff of a reed laid on a fire is burnt up, so all the sins of one who offers the Agnihotra knowing this thus are burnt up.
5.24.4: Therefore, even if one who knows thus should give the leavings of his food to a caṇḍāla, it would be offered in that caṇḍāla's Self, Vaiśvānara. On this there is this verse:
5.24.5: As here hungry children sit around their mother waiting, so all beings wait upon the Agnihotra of such a knower, they wait upon the Agnihotra.
6.1.1: There was Śvetaketu, son of Āruṇi. His father said to him: Śvetaketu, live the life of a brahmacārin, a student of the Veda. No one of our family, dear one, is like a brāhmaṇa in name only, without having studied.
6.1.2: He went to a teacher at twelve, and when he was twenty-four, having studied all the Vedas, he came home proud, thinking himself learned, and arrogant. His father said to him:
6.1.3: Śvetaketu, dear one, since you are now so proud, think yourself learned and are arrogant, did you also ask your teacher for that teaching by which the unheard becomes heard, the unthought becomes thought and the unknown becomes known? Śvetaketu asked: How, revered sir, is that teaching?
6.1.4: Uddālaka said: Dear one, it is as with one lump of clay: through it all that is made of clay becomes known; the modification is a name only, resting on speech, and the clay alone is true.
6.1.5: Dear one, it is as with one nugget of gold: through it all that is made of gold becomes known; the modification is a name only, resting on speech, and the gold alone is true.
6.1.6: Dear one, it is as with one nail-cutter: through it all that is made of iron becomes known; the modification is a name only, resting on speech, and the iron alone is true. Such, dear one, is that teaching.
6.1.7: Śvetaketu said: Surely those revered teachers of mine did not know this; had they known it, why would they not have told me? So may you yourself, revered sir, tell it to me. Uddālaka said: So be it, dear one.
6.2.1: In the beginning, dear one, this was Being alone, one only, without a second. On this some say: In the beginning this was non-being alone, one only, without a second, and from that non-being being was born.
6.2.2: Uddālaka said: But how, dear one, could that be so? How could being be born from non-being? No, dear one, in the beginning this was Being alone, one only, without a second.
6.2.3: It reflected: May I be many, may I be born. It brought forth tejas, fire. That tejas reflected: May I be many, may I be born. It brought forth water. That is why, wherever a person burns with grief or sweats, water arises there from tejas alone.
6.2.4: Those waters reflected: May we be many, may we be born. They brought forth food. That is why, wherever it rains, food is most plentiful there; food to eat arises from water alone.
6.3.1: Of these beings there are only three seeds: the egg-born, the live-born and the sprout-born.
6.3.2: That deity, Being, reflected: Well then, let me enter these three deities, tejas, water and food, by this living Self, and make name and form distinct.
6.3.3: Let me make each of them threefold. So that deity entered these three deities by this very living Self and made name and form distinct.
6.3.4: It made each of them threefold. And how, dear one, each of these three deities becomes threefold, learn that from me.
6.4.1: The red form of fire is the form of tejas, the white that of water, the black that of food. So the fireness of fire is gone: the modification is a name only, resting on speech, and the three forms alone are true.
6.4.2: The red form of the sun is the form of tejas, the white that of water, the black that of food. So the sunness of the sun is gone: the modification is a name only, resting on speech, and the three forms alone are true.
6.4.3: The red form of the moon is the form of tejas, the white that of water, the black that of food. So the moonness of the moon is gone: the modification is a name only, resting on speech, and the three forms alone are true.
6.4.4: The red form of lightning is the form of tejas, the white that of water, the black that of food. So the lightningness of lightning is gone: the modification is a name only, resting on speech, and the three forms alone are true.
6.4.5: Knowing this, the great householders and great Vedic scholars of old said: From now on none of our family will speak of anything as unheard, unthought or unknown. For from these three forms they knew it all.
6.4.6: Whatever looked red they knew to be the form of tejas; whatever looked white they knew to be the form of water; whatever looked black they knew to be the form of food.
6.4.7: Whatever seemed as though unknown they knew to be a combination of just these deities. And how, dear one, each of these three deities, on reaching a person, becomes threefold, learn that from me.
6.5.1: Food, when eaten, is divided in three. Its grossest part becomes faeces, its middle part flesh and its subtlest part the mind.
6.5.2: Water, when drunk, is divided in three. Its grossest part becomes urine, its middle part blood and its subtlest part prāṇa.
6.5.3: Tejas, when eaten in oil, ghee and the like, is divided in three. Its grossest part becomes bone, its middle part marrow and its subtlest part speech.
6.5.4: The mind, dear one, is indeed made of food, prāṇa of water, and speech of fire. Śvetaketu said: Revered sir, teach me further still. Uddālaka said: So be it, dear one.
6.6.1: Of curd, dear one, as it is churned, the finest part rises up; that becomes ghee.
6.6.2: In just the same way, dear one, of food as it is eaten, the finest part rises up; that becomes the mind.
6.6.3: Of water, dear one, as it is drunk, the finest part rises up; that becomes prāṇa, the breath of life.
6.6.4: Of fire, dear one, as it is eaten, the finest part rises up; that becomes speech.
6.6.5: The mind, dear one, is indeed made of food, prāṇa of water, and speech of fire. Śvetaketu said: Revered sir, teach me further still. Uddālaka said: So be it, dear one.
6.7.1: A man, dear one, is made of sixteen parts. Eat nothing for fifteen days; drink as much water as you wish. Prāṇa is made of water, so it will not be cut off in one who keeps drinking.
6.7.2: He did not eat for fifteen days. Then he came to him and said: What shall I recite, sir? Uddālaka said: The ṛk verses, dear one, the yajus formulas, the sāman chants. Śvetaketu said: They do not come to my mind at all, sir.
6.7.3: Uddālaka said to him: Dear one, just as of a great fire that has been heaped with fuel a single ember the size of a firefly may be left, with it one would burn not much beyond that; just so, dear one, of your sixteen parts only one part may be left, and with it you do not now grasp the Vedas. Eat; then you will understand me.
6.7.4: He ate. Then he came to him. Whatever Uddālaka asked him, he answered all of it.
6.7.5: Uddālaka said to him: Dear one, just as of a great fire that has been heaped with fuel a single ember the size of a firefly may be left, and if one heaped straw on it and made it blaze, with it one would burn far beyond that.
6.7.6: Just so, dear one, of your sixteen parts one part was left; fed with food, it blazed up, and with it you now grasp the Vedas. The mind, dear one, is indeed made of food, prāṇa of water, and speech of fire. Then he understood this from him; yes, he understood it.
6.8.1: Uddālaka Āruṇi said to his son Śvetaketu: Learn from me, dear one, the state of deep sleep. When a man here sleeps, as they say, then, dear one, he has become one with Being, sat; he has gone into his own Self. That is why they say of him svapiti, he sleeps: for he has gone (apīta) into his own (sva).
6.8.2: As a bird tied by a string flies off in every direction and, finding no resting place elsewhere, settles down at its very tether, just so, dear one, the mind flies off in every direction and, finding no resting place elsewhere, settles down in prāṇa alone; for the mind, dear one, is tethered to prāṇa.
6.8.3: Learn from me, dear one, hunger and thirst. When a man here is hungry, as they say, it is water that carries off what he has eaten. Just as people speak of a leader of cows, a leader of horses, a leader of men, so they call water aśanāyā, the leader of what is eaten. Know, dear one, that this body here is a sprout that has sprung up; it cannot be without a root.
6.8.4: Where else could its root be but in food? In just the same way, dear one, with food as the sprout, seek water as its root; with water as the sprout, dear one, seek fire as its root; with fire as the sprout, dear one, seek Being as its root. All these creatures, dear one, have Being as their root, Being as their abode, Being as their support.
6.8.5: And when a man here is thirsty, as they say, it is fire that carries off what he has drunk. Just as people speak of a leader of cows, a leader of horses, a leader of men, so they call fire udanyā, the leader of water. Know, dear one, that this same sprout has sprung up here; it cannot be without a root.
6.8.6: Where else could its root be but in water? With water as the sprout, dear one, seek fire as its root; with fire as the sprout, dear one, seek Being as its root. All these creatures, dear one, have Being as their root, Being as their abode, Being as their support. And how these three deities, dear one, on reaching a man, each become threefold has been told already. When this man, dear one, is departing, his speech is absorbed in the mind, the mind in prāṇa, prāṇa in fire, and fire in the highest deity.
6.8.7: That which is this finest essence, all this has it for its Self. That is the real; that is the Self. You are that, Śvetaketu. Śvetaketu said: Revered sir, teach me further still. Uddālaka said: So be it, dear one.
6.9.1: As the honey-makers, dear one, prepare honey by gathering the juices of many different trees and bringing that juice to oneness,
6.9.2: and as those juices there cannot tell themselves apart: I am this tree's juice, I am that tree's juice, just so, dear one, all these creatures, having merged in Being, do not know: We have merged in Being.
6.9.3: Whatever they are here, tiger or lion or wolf or boar or worm or moth or gnat or mosquito, that they become again.
6.9.4: That which is this finest essence, all this has it for its Self. That is the real; that is the Self. You are that, Śvetaketu. Śvetaketu said: Revered sir, teach me further still. Uddālaka said: So be it, dear one.
6.10.1: These rivers, dear one, flow, the eastern ones towards the east, the western ones towards the west. From the ocean they go into the ocean itself, and it becomes just the ocean. And as they there do not know: I am this one, I am this one,
6.10.2: just so, dear one, all these creatures, having come from Being, do not know: We have come from Being. Whatever they are here, tiger or lion or wolf or boar or worm or moth or gnat or mosquito, that they become again.
6.10.3: That which is this finest essence, all this has it for its Self. That is the real; that is the Self. You are that, Śvetaketu. Śvetaketu said: Revered sir, teach me further still. Uddālaka said: So be it, dear one.
6.11.1: Dear one, if someone strikes this great tree at its root, it would bleed sap but live; if someone strikes it in the middle, it would bleed but live; if someone strikes it at the top, it would bleed but live. Pervaded by its living Self, the jīva, it stands drinking deep and rejoicing.
6.11.2: When the jīva leaves one branch of it, that branch withers; it leaves a second, and that withers; it leaves a third, and that withers; it leaves the whole tree, and the whole tree withers.
6.11.3: Uddālaka said: Understand it to be just so, dear one. Bereft of the jīva, this body dies; the jīva does not die. That which is this finest essence, all this has it for its Self. That is the real; that is the Self. You are that, Śvetaketu. Śvetaketu said: Revered sir, teach me further still. Uddālaka said: So be it, dear one.
6.12.1: Bring a fruit of the banyan from over there. Śvetaketu said: Here it is, revered sir. — Break it. — It is broken, revered sir. — What do you see in it? — These seeds, quite tiny, revered sir. — My child, break one of these. — It is broken, revered sir. — What do you see in it? — Nothing at all, revered sir.
6.12.2: Uddālaka said to him: This finest essence, dear one, which you do not perceive, it is from this very finest essence, dear one, that this great banyan stands so. Have faith, dear one.
6.12.3: That which is this finest essence, all this has it for its Self. That is the real; that is the Self. You are that, Śvetaketu. Śvetaketu said: Revered sir, teach me further still. Uddālaka said: So be it, dear one.
6.13.1: Put this salt in water and come to me in the morning. He did so. Uddālaka said to him: The salt you put in the water last night, my child, bring it here. He felt about for it but did not find it,
6.13.2: for it had quite dissolved. Uddālaka said: My child, sip from the top of it. — How is it? — Salty. — Sip from the middle. — How is it? — Salty. — Sip from the bottom. — How is it? — Salty. — Throw it away and then come to me. He did so, and said: It is always there in it. Then Uddālaka said to him: Here indeed, dear one, you do not see Being; yet it is right here.
6.13.3: That which is this finest essence, all this has it for its Self. That is the real; that is the Self. You are that, Śvetaketu. Śvetaketu said: Revered sir, teach me further still. Uddālaka said: So be it, dear one.
6.14.1: Dear one, as someone might bring a man from the land of Gandhāra with his eyes blindfolded and then leave him in a place far from people, and as he there might cry out, facing east or north or south or west: I was brought here blindfolded, and blindfolded I have been left,
6.14.2: and as, if someone took off his blindfold and told him: Gandhāra lies this way; go this way, he, being wise and intelligent, would ask his way from village to village and reach Gandhāra itself; just so, here, a man who has a teacher knows. For him the delay lasts only so long as he is not freed; then he will reach Being.
6.14.3: That which is this finest essence, all this has it for its Self. That is the real; that is the Self. You are that, Śvetaketu. Śvetaketu said: Revered sir, teach me further still. Uddālaka said: So be it, dear one.
6.15.1: Dear one, around a man who is ill his kinsmen gather and ask: Do you know me? Do you know me? So long as his speech has not been absorbed in the mind, the mind in prāṇa, prāṇa in fire, and fire in the highest deity, so long he knows them.
6.15.2: Then, when his speech is absorbed in the mind, the mind in prāṇa, prāṇa in fire, and fire in the highest deity, he no longer knows them.
6.15.3: That which is this finest essence, all this has it for its Self. That is the real; that is the Self. You are that, Śvetaketu. Śvetaketu said: Revered sir, teach me further still. Uddālaka said: So be it, dear one.
6.16.1: Dear one, they bring in a man held by the hand, saying: He has taken something, he has committed theft; heat the axe for him. If he is the one who did it, by that very fact he makes himself false. Set on the false, hiding himself behind the false, he grasps the heated axe; he is burnt, and then he is put to death.
6.16.2: But if he is not the one who did it, by that very fact he makes himself true. Set on the true, hiding himself behind the true, he grasps the heated axe; he is not burnt, and then he is set free.
6.16.3: Just as that man, holding to the true, is not burnt there, so is it with the one who knows the true. All this has it for its Self. That is the real; that is the Self. You are that, Śvetaketu. Then he understood this from him; yes, he understood it.
7.1.1: Saying: Teach me, revered sir, Nārada came to Sanatkumāra as a pupil. Sanatkumāra said to him: Come to me by telling me what you know; then I shall tell you what lies beyond it. Nārada said:
7.1.2: Revered sir, I have studied the Ṛgveda, the Yajurveda, the Sāmaveda, the Atharvaveda as the fourth, history and the Purāṇas as the fifth, the Veda of the Vedas (grammar), the rites for the ancestors, mathematics, the reading of portents, the science of treasures, logic, the science of conduct, etymology, the auxiliaries of the Veda, the science of spirits, archery, astronomy, the science of serpents and the fine arts. All this, revered sir, I have studied.
7.1.3: Yet, revered sir, I am only one who knows the mantras, not one who knows the Self. For I have heard from those like you, sir, that one who knows the Self passes beyond sorrow. Revered sir, I am in sorrow; take me, sir, to the far shore of sorrow. Sanatkumāra said to him: Whatever you have studied is only name.
7.1.4: The Ṛgveda is name, and so are the Yajurveda, the Sāmaveda, the Atharvaveda as the fourth, history and the Purāṇas as the fifth, the Veda of the Vedas (grammar), the rites for the ancestors, mathematics, the reading of portents, the science of treasures, logic, the science of conduct, etymology, the auxiliaries of the Veda, the science of spirits, archery, astronomy, the science of serpents and the fine arts: all this is only name. Meditate on name.
7.1.5: He who meditates on name as Brahman, the ultimate reality, can move as he wishes as far as name reaches — he who meditates on name as Brahman. Nārada asked: Revered sir, is there anything greater than name? Sanatkumāra said: There is indeed something greater than name. Nārada said: Revered sir, tell me that.
7.2.1: Sanatkumāra said: Speech, indeed, is greater than name. It is speech that makes known the Ṛgveda, the Yajurveda, the Sāmaveda, the Atharvaveda as the fourth, history and the Purāṇas as the fifth, the Veda of the Vedas (grammar), the rites for the ancestors, mathematics, the reading of portents, the science of treasures, logic, the science of conduct, etymology, the auxiliaries of the Veda, the science of spirits, archery, astronomy, the science of serpents and the fine arts, and heaven and earth, wind and space, water and fire, gods and men, cattle and birds, grass and trees, beasts of prey down to worms, moths and ants, right and wrong, true and false, good and bad, the pleasing and the unpleasing. Were there no speech, neither right nor wrong would be known, neither true nor false, neither good nor bad, neither the pleasing nor the unpleasing. Speech alone makes all this known. Meditate on speech.
7.2.2: He who meditates on speech as Brahman can move as he wishes as far as speech reaches — he who meditates on speech as Brahman. Nārada asked: Revered sir, is there anything greater than speech? Sanatkumāra said: There is indeed something greater than speech. Nārada said: Revered sir, tell me that.
7.3.1: Sanatkumāra said: Mind, indeed, is greater than speech. Just as a closed fist holds two āmalaka fruits, or two jujubes, or two vibhītaka nuts, so mind holds speech and name within it. When a man resolves in his mind: Let me study the mantras, he then studies them; let me perform rites, he then performs them; let me seek sons and cattle, he then seeks them; let me seek this world and the next, he then seeks them. For mind is the Self, mind is the world, mind is Brahman. Meditate on mind.
7.3.2: He who meditates on mind as Brahman can move as he wishes as far as mind reaches — he who meditates on mind as Brahman. Nārada asked: Revered sir, is there anything greater than mind? Sanatkumāra said: There is indeed something greater than mind. Nārada said: Revered sir, tell me that.
7.4.1: Sanatkumāra said: Will, indeed, is greater than mind. When a man wills, he then thinks in his mind, then sets speech going, and sets it going in name. In name the mantras become one, and in the mantras the rites.
7.4.2: All these have will as their one meeting-place, will as their self, and rest in will. Heaven and earth willed, as it were; wind and space willed, as it were; water and fire willed, as it were. By their willing, rain is made possible; by the willing of rain, food is made possible; by the willing of food, the life-breaths are made possible; by the willing of the life-breaths, the mantras are made possible; by the willing of the mantras, the rites are made possible; by the willing of the rites, the world is made possible; by the willing of the world, everything is made possible. Such is will. Meditate on will.
7.4.3: He who meditates on will as Brahman attains the worlds shaped by will: firm himself, he attains firm worlds; established himself, established worlds; untroubled himself, untroubled worlds; he can move as he wishes as far as will reaches — he who meditates on will as Brahman. Nārada asked: Revered sir, is there anything greater than will? Sanatkumāra said: There is indeed something greater than will. Nārada said: Revered sir, tell me that.
7.5.1: Sanatkumāra said: Awareness, indeed, is greater than will. When a man becomes aware, he then wills, then thinks in his mind, then sets speech going, and sets it going in name. In name the mantras become one, and in the mantras the rites.
7.5.2: All these have awareness as their one meeting-place, awareness as their self, and rest in awareness. So even if a man knows much, if he lacks awareness, people say of him: He is nobody, and what he knows is nothing; were he truly learned, he would not be so lacking in awareness. But if a man who knows little has awareness, it is to him that people wish to listen. For awareness is the one meeting-place of all these, awareness is their self, awareness is their support. Meditate on awareness.
7.5.3: He who meditates on awareness as Brahman attains worlds built up and full: firm himself, he attains firm worlds; established himself, established worlds; untroubled himself, untroubled worlds; he can move as he wishes as far as awareness reaches — he who meditates on awareness as Brahman. Nārada asked: Revered sir, is there anything greater than awareness? Sanatkumāra said: There is indeed something greater than awareness. Nārada said: Revered sir, tell me that.
7.6.1: Sanatkumāra said: Contemplation, indeed, is greater than awareness. The earth contemplates, as it were; the mid-space contemplates, as it were; heaven contemplates, as it were; the waters contemplate, as it were; the mountains contemplate, as it were; gods and men contemplate, as it were. So those among men here who reach greatness seem to have gained a share of the fruit of contemplation. The petty are quarrelsome, talebearers and slanderers; but the eminent seem to have gained a share of the fruit of contemplation. Meditate on contemplation.
7.6.2: He who meditates on contemplation as Brahman can move as he wishes as far as contemplation reaches — he who meditates on contemplation as Brahman. Nārada asked: Revered sir, is there anything greater than contemplation? Sanatkumāra said: There is indeed something greater than contemplation. Nārada said: Revered sir, tell me that.
7.7.1: Sanatkumāra said: Understanding, indeed, is greater than contemplation. By understanding a man understands the Ṛgveda, the Yajurveda, the Sāmaveda, the Atharvaveda as the fourth, history and the Purāṇas as the fifth, the Veda of the Vedas (grammar), the rites for the ancestors, mathematics, the reading of portents, the science of treasures, logic, the science of conduct, etymology, the auxiliaries of the Veda, the science of spirits, archery, astronomy, the science of serpents and the fine arts, and heaven and earth, wind and space, water and fire, gods and men, cattle and birds, grass and trees, beasts of prey down to worms, moths and ants, right and wrong, true and false, good and bad, the pleasing and the unpleasing, food and taste, this world and the next: by understanding alone he understands them. Meditate on understanding.
7.7.2: He who meditates on understanding as Brahman attains worlds full of understanding and knowledge; he can move as he wishes as far as understanding reaches — he who meditates on understanding as Brahman. Nārada asked: Revered sir, is there anything greater than understanding? Sanatkumāra said: There is indeed something greater than understanding. Nārada said: Revered sir, tell me that.
7.8.1: Sanatkumāra said: Strength, indeed, is greater than understanding. One strong man makes even a hundred men of understanding tremble. When a man is strong, he rises up; rising, he serves; serving, he draws near; drawing near, he becomes one who sees, who hears, who reflects, who understands, who acts and who knows. By strength the earth stands; by strength the mid-space, by strength heaven, by strength the mountains, by strength gods and men, by strength cattle and birds, grass and trees, beasts of prey down to worms, moths and ants; by strength the world stands. Meditate on strength.
7.8.2: He who meditates on strength as Brahman can move as he wishes as far as strength reaches — he who meditates on strength as Brahman. Nārada asked: Revered sir, is there anything greater than strength? Sanatkumāra said: There is indeed something greater than strength. Nārada said: Revered sir, tell me that.
7.9.1: Sanatkumāra said: Food, indeed, is greater than strength. So if a man does not eat for ten nights, then even if he lives, he becomes one who does not see, hear, reflect, understand, act or know. But when food comes to him, he becomes one who sees, who hears, who reflects, who understands, who acts and who knows. Meditate on food.
7.9.2: He who meditates on food as Brahman attains worlds rich in food and drink; he can move as he wishes as far as food reaches — he who meditates on food as Brahman. Nārada asked: Revered sir, is there anything greater than food? Sanatkumāra said: There is indeed something greater than food. Nārada said: Revered sir, tell me that.
7.10.1: Sanatkumāra said: Water, indeed, is greater than food. So when the rains are poor, living beings fall sick, thinking: Food will be scarce. And when the rains are good, living beings rejoice, thinking: Food will be plentiful. All these are simply water in bodily form: this earth, the mid-space, heaven, the mountains, gods and men, cattle and birds, grass and trees, beasts of prey down to worms, moths and ants; all these are water in bodily form. Meditate on water.
7.10.2: He who meditates on water as Brahman obtains all his desires and is content; he can move as he wishes as far as water reaches — he who meditates on water as Brahman. Nārada asked: Revered sir, is there anything greater than water? Sanatkumāra said: There is indeed something greater than water. Nārada said: Revered sir, tell me that.
7.11.1: Sanatkumāra said: Fire, indeed, is greater than water. It is this fire that, holding the air still, heats up space all round. Then people say: It is burning, it is scorching; it will rain. Fire first shows itself, and then brings forth water. It is this same fire with which thunderclaps roll along with lightning that flashes upward and across; so people say: There is lightning, there is thunder; it will rain. Fire first shows itself, and then brings forth water. Meditate on fire.
7.11.2: He who meditates on fire as Brahman becomes radiant, and attains radiant worlds, full of light and free of darkness; he can move as he wishes as far as fire reaches — he who meditates on fire as Brahman. Nārada asked: Revered sir, is there anything greater than fire? Sanatkumāra said: There is indeed something greater than fire. Nārada said: Revered sir, tell me that.
7.12.1: Sanatkumāra said: Space, indeed, is greater than fire. Sun and moon alike are in space, and lightning, the stars and fire. By means of space one calls out, by means of space one hears, by means of space one hears an answer. One delights in space, and one finds no delight in space; one is born in space, and all things grow towards space. Meditate on space.
7.12.2: He who meditates on space as Brahman attains worlds that are spacious, full of light, free from crowding and wide to range in; he can move as he wishes as far as space reaches — he who meditates on space as Brahman. Nārada asked: Revered sir, is there anything greater than space? Sanatkumāra said: There is indeed something greater than space. Nārada said: Revered sir, tell me that.
7.13.1: Sanatkumāra said: Memory, indeed, is greater than space. So even if many people are sitting together, if they have no memory, they would not hear anyone, nor reflect, nor understand. Only when they remember would they hear, reflect and understand. By memory a man knows his sons; by memory, his cattle. Meditate on memory.
7.13.2: He who meditates on memory as Brahman can move as he wishes as far as memory reaches — he who meditates on memory as Brahman. Nārada asked: Revered sir, is there anything greater than memory? Sanatkumāra said: There is indeed something greater than memory. Nārada said: Revered sir, tell me that.
7.14.1: Sanatkumāra said: Hope, indeed, is greater than memory. Kindled by hope, the one who remembers studies the mantras, performs rites, seeks sons and cattle, and seeks this world and the next. Meditate on hope.
7.14.2: He who meditates on hope as Brahman — through hope all his desires prosper, and his prayers never fail; he can move as he wishes as far as hope reaches — he who meditates on hope as Brahman. Nārada asked: Revered sir, is there anything greater than hope? Sanatkumāra said: There is indeed something greater than hope. Nārada said: Revered sir, tell me that.
7.15.1: Sanatkumāra said: Prāṇa, the breath of life, is indeed greater than hope. As the spokes of a wheel are fixed in its hub, so everything is fixed in this prāṇa. Prāṇa moves by prāṇa; prāṇa gives prāṇa, and gives it to prāṇa. Prāṇa is father, prāṇa is mother, prāṇa is brother, prāṇa is sister, prāṇa is teacher, prāṇa is brāhmaṇa.
7.15.2: If a man answers his father or mother, brother or sister, teacher or a brāhmaṇa somewhat harshly, people say to him: Shame on you! You are a slayer of your father, you are a slayer of your mother, you are a slayer of your brother, you are a slayer of your sister, you are a slayer of your teacher, you are a slayer of a brāhmaṇa.
7.15.3: But once the breath of life has left them, even if he heaps them together with a spit and burns them up, tossing their limbs about, no one would say to him: You are a slayer of your father; nor: a slayer of your mother; nor: a slayer of your brother; nor: a slayer of your sister; nor: a slayer of your teacher; nor: a slayer of a brāhmaṇa.
7.15.4: For it is prāṇa that becomes all these. He who sees thus, reflects thus and understands thus becomes an ativādin, one who speaks of what lies beyond all. If people say to him: You are an ativādin, he should say: I am an ativādin; he should not deny it.
7.16.1: Sanatkumāra said: But he truly speaks beyond all who speaks beyond all by the truth. Nārada said: Then, revered sir, let me speak beyond all by the truth. Sanatkumāra said: But it is the truth itself that one must seek to know. Nārada said: Revered sir, I seek to know the truth.
7.17.1: Sanatkumāra said: Only when one understands does one speak the truth. One who does not understand does not speak the truth; only one who understands speaks the truth. But it is understanding that one must seek to know. Nārada said: Revered sir, I seek to know understanding.
7.18.1: Sanatkumāra said: Only when one reflects does one understand. One who has not reflected does not understand; only by reflecting does one understand. But it is reflection that one must seek to know. Nārada said: Revered sir, I seek to know reflection.
7.19.1: Sanatkumāra said: Only when one has faith does one reflect. One without faith does not reflect; only one who has faith reflects. But it is faith that one must seek to know. Nārada said: Revered sir, I seek to know faith.
7.20.1: Sanatkumāra said: Only when one is steadfast does one have faith. One who is not steadfast does not have faith; only one who is steadfast has faith. But it is steadfastness that one must seek to know. Nārada said: Revered sir, I seek to know steadfastness.
7.21.1: Sanatkumāra said: Only when one acts is one steadfast. No one is steadfast without acting; only by acting is one steadfast. But it is action that one must seek to know. Nārada said: Revered sir, I seek to know action.
7.22.1: Sanatkumāra said: Only when one gains happiness does one act. No one acts having gained no happiness; only having gained happiness does one act. But it is happiness that one must seek to know. Nārada said: Revered sir, I seek to know happiness.
7.23.1: Sanatkumāra said: That which is the infinite (bhūman) is happiness. There is no happiness in the small; the infinite alone is happiness. But it is the infinite that one must seek to know. Nārada said: Revered sir, I seek to know the infinite.
7.24.1: Sanatkumāra said: Where one sees no other thing, hears no other, knows no other, that is the infinite. But where one sees another thing, hears another, knows another, that is the small. That which is the infinite is immortal; that which is small is mortal. Nārada asked: Revered sir, on what does the infinite rest? Sanatkumāra said: On its own greatness — or rather, not even on greatness.
7.24.2: Here people call cows and horses greatness, and elephants and gold, servants and wives, fields and houses. Sanatkumāra said: I do not speak of it in that way, for there one thing rests on another. This is what I say:
7.25.1: He indeed is below, he above, he behind, he in front, he to the south, he to the north; he indeed is all this. Now next comes the teaching in terms of I (ahaṅkārādeśa): I indeed am below, I above, I behind, I in front, I to the south, I to the north; I indeed am all this.
7.25.2: Now next comes the teaching in terms of the Self, the ātman (ātmādeśa): The Self indeed is below, the Self above, the Self behind, the Self in front, the Self to the south, the Self to the north; the Self indeed is all this. He who sees thus, reflects thus and understands thus delights in the Self, sports with the Self, has his union with the Self and his joy in the Self. He becomes self-ruled (svarāṭ), and he can move as he wishes in all worlds. But those who know otherwise than this are ruled by another; their worlds perish, and they cannot move as they wish in any of the worlds.
7.26.1: For him who sees thus, reflects thus and understands thus, prāṇa, the breath of life, comes from the Self; from the Self come hope, memory, space, fire and water; from the Self, appearing and vanishing; from the Self come food, strength, understanding, contemplation, awareness, will, mind, speech, name, the mantras and the rites. From the Self indeed comes all this.
7.26.2: On this there is a verse: The one who sees does not see death, nor illness, nor any sorrow. The one who sees sees everything, and attains everything in every way. He is onefold, he is threefold, fivefold, sevenfold and ninefold; and again he is called elevenfold, and a hundred and ten and one, and twenty thousand. When food is pure, the mind is pure; when the mind is pure, memory becomes firm; when memory is gained, all the knots are loosened. To Nārada, whose stains had been wiped away, the revered Sanatkumāra showed the far shore of darkness. Him they call Skanda; him they call Skanda.
8.1.1: Now, in this city of Brahman there is a small lotus, a dwelling, and within it a small inner space. What is within that is what should be sought; that indeed is what one should seek to know.
8.1.2: If the pupils should say to him: In this city of Brahman there is this small lotus, a dwelling, and within it a small inner space; what is there in it that should be sought, that one should seek to know? — he should say:
8.1.3: As vast as this space is, so vast is the space within the heart. Both heaven and earth are held right within it, fire and air both, sun and moon both, lightning and the stars; whatever one has here and whatever one has not, all of it is held within it.
8.1.4: If they should say to him: If all this is held in this city of Brahman, all beings and all desires, then when old age overtakes it or it perishes, what is left after that?
8.1.5: He should say: This does not grow old with its old age, nor is it slain by its slaying. This is the true city of Brahman; in it the desires are held. This is the Self, free from evil, ageless, deathless, free from sorrow, free from hunger and free from thirst, whose desires are true and whose resolves are true. For it is just as here: people follow as they are commanded, and whatever border region they long for, whatever country, whatever piece of land, on that they live dependent.
8.1.6: Just as here a world won by work comes to an end, so in the next a world won by merit comes to an end. So those who depart from here without having found the Self and these true desires cannot move as they wish in any of the worlds. But those who depart from here having found the Self and these true desires can move as they wish in all worlds.
8.2.1: If he desires the world of the fathers, at his mere will the fathers rise up before him; possessed of that world of the fathers, he is exalted.
8.2.2: And if he desires the world of the mothers, at his mere will the mothers rise up before him; possessed of that world of the mothers, he is exalted.
8.2.3: And if he desires the world of brothers, at his mere will brothers rise up before him; possessed of that world of brothers, he is exalted.
8.2.4: And if he desires the world of sisters, at his mere will sisters rise up before him; possessed of that world of sisters, he is exalted.
8.2.5: And if he desires the world of friends, at his mere will friends rise up before him; possessed of that world of friends, he is exalted.
8.2.6: And if he desires the world of perfumes and garlands, at his mere will perfumes and garlands rise up before him; possessed of that world of perfumes and garlands, he is exalted.
8.2.7: And if he desires the world of food and drink, at his mere will food and drink rise up before him; possessed of that world of food and drink, he is exalted.
8.2.8: And if he desires the world of song and music, at his mere will song and music rise up before him; possessed of that world of song and music, he is exalted.
8.2.9: And if he desires the world of women, at his mere will women rise up before him; possessed of that world of women, he is exalted.
8.2.10: Whatever place he longs for, whatever desire he desires, it rises up before him at his mere will; possessed of it, he is exalted.
8.3.1: These true desires are covered by the untrue. Though they are true, the untrue is their covering; for whoever of one's own departs from here, one does not get him back here to see.
8.3.2: And those of his who are living here and those who are dead, and anything else he wishes for and does not get — all that he finds by going here; for here are these true desires of his, covered by the untrue. Just as people who do not know the ground may walk over a hidden treasure of gold buried beneath them again and again and not find it, so all these creatures go into this world of Brahman day after day and do not find it; for they are carried away by the untrue.
8.3.3: This Self is in the heart. And this is the meaning of the word: hṛdi ayam, this is in the heart; therefore it is hṛdayam, the heart. He who knows thus goes day after day to the heavenly world.
8.3.4: And this serene one (samprasāda), rising out of this body and attaining the supreme light, comes forth in its own form. This is the Self, he said. This is the immortal, the fearless; this is Brahman. The name of this Brahman is the True (satyam).
8.3.5: These are the three syllables: sa, tī, yam. Of them, sat is the immortal; ti is the mortal; and by yam one holds the two together. Because by it one holds the two together, it is yam. He who knows thus goes day after day to the heavenly world.
8.4.1: Now the Self is a dam (setu), a support that keeps these worlds from breaking apart. Day and night do not cross this dam, nor old age, nor death, nor sorrow, nor good deeds, nor evil deeds. All evils turn back from it, for this world of Brahman is free from evil.
8.4.2: Therefore, having crossed this dam, one who is blind is blind no more, one who is wounded is wounded no more, one who is afflicted is afflicted no more. Therefore, on crossing this dam, even the night turns into day; for this world of Brahman shines once and for ever.
8.4.3: So those who find this world of Brahman through brahmacarya, the chaste life of a student — theirs alone is this world of Brahman; they can move as they wish in all worlds.
8.5.1: And what people call sacrifice (yajña) is brahmacarya; for it is through brahmacarya that one who knows (yo jñātā) finds that world. And what people call worship (iṣṭa) is brahmacarya; for it is by worshipping (iṣṭvā) through brahmacarya that one finds the Self.
8.5.2: And what people call the long sacrificial session (sattrāyaṇa) is brahmacarya; for through brahmacarya one finds from the Real (sat), the Self, protection (trāṇa) for oneself. And what people call silence (mauna) is brahmacarya; for having found the Self through brahmacarya, one reflects (manute) on it.
8.5.3: And what people call the course of fasting (anāśakāyana) is brahmacarya; for this Self, which one finds through brahmacarya, does not perish (na naśyati). And what people call life in the forest (araṇyāyana) is brahmacarya. There, in the world of Brahman, in the third heaven from here, are the two oceans Ara and Ṇya; there is the lake Airaṃmadīya, full of refreshing drink that gladdens; there is the aśvattha tree that pours soma (somasavana); there is Aparājitā, the unconquered city of Brahmā, and the golden hall built by the Lord.
8.5.4: So those who find these two oceans, Ara and Ṇya, in the world of Brahman through brahmacarya — theirs alone is this world of Brahman; they can move as they wish in all worlds.
8.6.1: Now these channels (nāḍīs) of the heart are filled with a fine essence that is tawny, white, blue, yellow and red. That sun is indeed tawny; this is white, this is blue, this is yellow, this is red.
8.6.2: Just as a long highway runs to both villages, this one and that one, so these rays of the sun run to both worlds, this one and that one. They spread out from that sun and enter these channels; they spread out from these channels and enter that sun.
8.6.3: So when one is asleep in this way, with all his senses gathered in, wholly serene, and knows no dream, he has then entered these channels. No evil touches him then, for he is then filled with radiance.
8.6.4: And when a man has been brought to weakness, those sitting around him say: Do you know me? Do you know me? So long as he has not departed from this body, he knows them.
8.6.5: Then, when he departs from this body, he climbs upward by these very rays. Meditating on Om, he goes upward, or else goes another way. In the time it takes to cast the mind, he reaches the sun. That indeed is the door of the world: the way in for those who know, a barrier for those who do not.
8.6.6: On this there is a verse: A hundred and one are the channels of the heart; of them, one goes out towards the crown of the head. Going up by it, one reaches immortality; the others, running every way, serve only for departing, serve only for departing.
8.7.1: The Self that is free from evil, ageless, deathless, free from sorrow, free from hunger and free from thirst, whose desires are true and whose resolves are true: that is the one to be sought, that is the one to be known. He gains all worlds and all desires who has found that Self and knows it. So Prajāpati once said.
8.7.2: Both the gods and the demons heard of it. They said: Come, let us seek that Self, by seeking which one gains all worlds and all desires. So Indra set out from among the gods, and Virocana from among the demons. Without a word to each other, the two came to Prajāpati with fuel in their hands.
8.7.3: The two lived there as students, in brahmacarya, for thirty-two years. Then Prajāpati asked them: Wishing for what have you lived here? They said: The Self that is free from evil, ageless, deathless, free from sorrow, free from hunger and free from thirst, whose desires are true and whose resolves are true: that is the one to be sought, that is the one to be known; he gains all worlds and all desires who has found that Self and knows it. People repeat this as your word, revered sir. Wishing for that Self we have lived here.
8.7.4: Prajāpati said to them: The person who is seen in the eye is the Self. This is the immortal, the fearless; this is Brahman. Then they asked: Revered sir, the one who is seen in water and the one who is seen in a mirror: which of these is he? Prajāpati said: It is this very one who is seen in all these.
8.8.1: Look at yourselves in a pan of water, and whatever you do not understand of the Self, tell me. They looked in the pan of water. Prajāpati asked them: What do you see? They said: Revered sir, we see the whole of ourselves, a likeness down to the very hairs and nails.
8.8.2: Prajāpati said to them: Adorn yourselves well, put on fine clothes, groom yourselves, and then look in the pan of water. They adorned themselves well, put on fine clothes, groomed themselves and looked in the pan of water. Prajāpati asked them: What do you see?
8.8.3: They said: Revered sir, just as we two are well adorned, finely dressed and groomed, so, revered sir, these two are well adorned, finely dressed and groomed. Prajāpati said: This is the Self. This is the immortal, the fearless; this is Brahman. The two went away content at heart.
8.8.4: Looking after them as they went, Prajāpati said: They go without having grasped the Self, without having found it. Those who hold this as their secret teaching (upaniṣad), whether gods or demons, will come to ruin. Virocana, content at heart, went to the demons and declared to them this teaching: Here the self (the body) alone is to be honoured, the self alone is to be served. Honouring the self here and serving the self, one gains both worlds, this one and the one beyond.
8.8.5: That is why even now, here, of one who does not give, has no faith and does not sacrifice, people say: How demonic he is! For this is the teaching of the demons. They dress the body of the dead with what is got as alms, with clothing and with ornaments, for they think that by this they will win the world beyond.
8.9.1: But Indra, before he had even reached the gods, saw this danger: Just as this self is well adorned when this body is well adorned, finely dressed when it is finely dressed and groomed when it is groomed, so it is blind when the body is blind, one-eyed when it is one-eyed and maimed when it is maimed. It perishes as soon as the body perishes. I see nothing worth having in this.
8.9.2: He came back, fuel in hand. Prajāpati said to him: Maghavan, you went away content at heart, together with Virocana; wishing for what have you come back? He said: Revered sir, just as this self is well adorned when this body is well adorned, finely dressed when it is finely dressed and groomed when it is groomed, so it is blind when the body is blind, one-eyed when it is one-eyed and maimed when it is maimed. It perishes as soon as the body perishes. I see nothing worth having in this.
8.9.3: Prajāpati said: It is just so, Maghavan. But I will explain this same Self to you further. Live here another thirty-two years. He lived there another thirty-two years. Then Prajāpati said to him:
8.10.1: The one who moves about glorified in dream is the Self, he said. This is the immortal, the fearless; this is Brahman. He went away content at heart. But before he had even reached the gods, he saw this danger: Even if this body is blind, that self is not blind; if the body is one-eyed, it is not one-eyed; it is not marred by the body's faults.
8.10.2: It is not killed when the body is killed, nor made one-eyed by its being one-eyed; yet it is as if they kill it, as if they chase it away; it becomes as it were one who feels what is unpleasant, and even weeps, as it were. I see nothing worth having in this.
8.10.3: He came back, fuel in hand. Prajāpati said to him: Maghavan, you went away content at heart; wishing for what have you come back? He said: Revered sir, even if this body is blind, that self is not blind; if the body is one-eyed, it is not one-eyed; it is not marred by the body's faults.
8.10.4: It is not killed when the body is killed, nor made one-eyed by its being one-eyed; yet it is as if they kill it, as if they chase it away; it becomes as it were one who feels what is unpleasant, and even weeps, as it were. I see nothing worth having in this. Prajāpati said: It is just so, Maghavan. But I will explain this same Self to you further. Live here another thirty-two years. He lived there another thirty-two years. Then Prajāpati said to him:
8.11.1: When one is asleep in this way, with all his senses gathered in, wholly serene, and knows no dream, that is the Self, he said. This is the immortal, the fearless; this is Brahman. He went away content at heart. But before he had even reached the gods, he saw this danger: Truly, he does not now know himself in this way: This am I; nor does he know these beings. He has gone, as it were, into destruction. I see nothing worth having in this.
8.11.2: He came back, fuel in hand. Prajāpati said to him: Maghavan, you went away content at heart; wishing for what have you come back? He said: Revered sir, truly, he does not now know himself in this way: This am I; nor does he know these beings. He has gone, as it were, into destruction. I see nothing worth having in this.
8.11.3: Prajāpati said: It is just so, Maghavan. But I will explain this same Self to you further, and nothing other than this. Live here five more years. He lived there five more years. These made a hundred and one. That is why people say: Maghavan lived as a student with Prajāpati for a hundred and one years. Then Prajāpati said to him:
8.12.1: Maghavan, this body is mortal; it is held fast by death. It is the abode of this immortal, bodiless Self. One who has a body is held fast by the pleasant and the unpleasant; as long as one has a body, there is no getting free of the pleasant and the unpleasant. But the pleasant and the unpleasant do not touch one who is bodiless.
8.12.2: The wind is bodiless; cloud, lightning and thunder, these too are bodiless. Just as these rise out of that space, attain the supreme light and come forth each in its own form,
8.12.3: just so this serene one (samprasāda), rising out of this body and attaining the supreme light, comes forth in its own form. He is the highest person. There he moves about, laughing, playing and rejoicing with women, carriages or kinsfolk, not remembering this body that clings to him. As a draught animal is yoked to a cart, so prāṇa, the life-breath, is yoked to this body.
8.12.4: Now where the eye is set in the space of the pupil, there is the person of the eye; the eye is for seeing. He who knows: Let me smell this, is the Self; the nose is for smelling. He who knows: Let me say this, is the Self; speech is for speaking. He who knows: Let me hear this, is the Self; the ear is for hearing.
8.12.5: He who knows: Let me think this, is the Self; the mind is his divine eye. With this divine eye, the mind, he sees these objects of desire in the world of Brahman and rejoices.
8.12.6: The gods meditate on this Self; therefore all worlds and all desires are theirs. He gains all worlds and all desires who has found that Self and knows it. So said Prajāpati, so said Prajāpati.
8.13.1: From the dark I go to the many-coloured; from the many-coloured I go to the dark. Shaking off evil as a horse shakes off its hairs, freeing myself as the moon frees itself from the mouth of Rāhu, shaking off the body, I, my self fulfilled, reach the uncreated world of Brahman; I reach it.
8.14.1: What is called space (ākāśa) is what brings forth name and form; that within which they lie is Brahman, that is the immortal, that is the Self. I go to the hall of Prajāpati, to his dwelling. I become the glory of the brāhmaṇas, the glory of kings, the glory of the vaiśyas. I wish to attain glory; I am the glory of glories. May I never go to the reddish-white, the toothless, the toothless, the reddish-white, the slimy; may I never go to it.
8.15.1: Brahmā taught this to Prajāpati, Prajāpati to Manu, and Manu to all creatures. He who has learnt the Veda from the teacher's family as the rules prescribe, in the time left over from his work for the teacher; who has come home and lives as a householder, reciting his Veda in a clean place and training his sons and pupils in righteousness; who has drawn all his senses into the Self, and harms no creature except where the scriptures allow: he who lives thus all his life reaches the world of Brahman, and does not return again, does not return again.

shanti.1: The śānti pāṭha of the Upaniṣads of the Sāmaveda (Kena, Chāndogya). Peace is said three times, for freedom from the troubles that come from oneself, from other beings and from the powers of nature.
1.1.10: Upaniṣad here is read with Śaṅkara as yoga, concentrated meditation; some take it as the secret teaching about the syllable.
1.2.1: Śaṅkara reads the gods and the demons as the workings of the senses within every person: those lit by scripture, and their natural dark tendencies.
1.6.6: Śaṅkara takes golden to mean radiant like gold, not made of gold.
1.6.7: Kapyāsa is read here with Śaṅkara; Rāmānuja takes it as a lotus opened by the sun.
1.6.8: Geṣṇau is read with Śaṅkara as two joints; some take it as two singers.
1.7.1: Śaṅkara takes prāṇa here as the sense of smell together with the breath.
1.9.1: Śaṅkara takes ākāśa here to mean the supreme Self.
1.10.1: Āṭikī is read with Śaṅkara as a young girl; some take it as the wife's name.
1.12.1: Śaṅkara takes Baka Dālbhya and Glāva Maitreya as two names of one sage, belonging to two family lines; the verbs of the mantra are singular.
1.12.2: Śaṅkara says a deity or a sage, pleased by the recitation, took the form of the white dog to favour the sage; or else the chief prāṇa, with speech and the other vital powers, took the form of the dogs.
1.12.5: Śaṅkara takes god, Varuṇa, Prajāpati and Savitṛ all as names of the sun: god for his shining, Varuṇa for his rain, Prajāpati for protecting creatures, Savitṛ for bringing all things forth.
2.9.8: Śaṅkara: in the rite for the ancestors, father, grandfather and great-grandfather are set down on darbha grass, or the rice-balls offered to them are laid there.
2.11.2: The usual sense of jyok is for a long time (he lives long); Śaṅkara takes it as brightly. The phrase recurs in the following sections in the same sense.
2.19.2: The text has majjñaḥ, marrow; Śaṅkara takes it as meat, its plural taking in fish as well.
2.23.1: Śaṅkara takes the one established in Brahman to be the renunciate who has left all ritual action; another view, which he rejects, includes anyone in any stage of life who is established in Brahman.
2.24.4: Śaṅkara takes this chant as addressed to Agni. A sāman draws the words out and inserts sounds such as hum: rā … hum … ā-jyā-yo-ā is rājyāya, for kingship; the later chants sing vairājyāya, svārājyāya and sāmrājyāya in the same way.
2.24.7: Śaṅkara takes the Āgnīdhrīya fire here to be the southern fire, the Dakṣiṇāgni.
3.1.2: With Śaṅkara, the Ṛgveda here means the rites the Ṛgveda prescribes, and the waters are the soma, ghee and milk offered in them, whose essence the ṛk verses draw as bees draw nectar.
3.5.1: Since the topic is the sacred word, Śaṅkara takes Brahman here as the syllable Om; some read it as the Veda or as the supreme Brahman.
3.6.2: With Śaṅkara, when it is not their time to enjoy it the gods withdraw into this form and rest, and when the time comes they rise from it, eager to enjoy.
3.7.4: Śaṅkara explains the sun's rising in the south, west or north as it is seen from the cities of the gods; the sun's course itself does not change.
3.11.2: Śaṅkara reads this as the answer of a knower returned from the world of Brahmā, asked whether the sun rises and sets there; he calls the gods to witness.
3.12.1: The name Gāyatrī is explained from gāyati, sings (speech names all beings), and trāyate, protects.
3.12.5: Per Śaṅkara, as a metre the Gāyatrī has four feet of six syllables each, and it is sixfold as speech, beings, earth, body, heart and the prāṇas.
3.12.6: The verse is from the Puruṣasūkta (Ṛgveda 10.90.3). Śaṅkara takes in heaven as in its own shining nature.
3.14.1: Tajjalān is a coined word: taj-ja, born from it; tal-la, dissolving into it; tad-an, living in it.
3.15.3: In place of so-and-so the father says his son's name three times; per Śaṅkara this rite is for the son's long life.
3.17.5: Soṣyati and asoṣṭa are said both of a birth and of pressing the soma; with Śaṅkara, this sameness of words too makes a man the sacrifice.
3.17.7: Only the opening words of the first ṛk are given here; with Śaṅkara, the whole ṛk says: then (the pure in mind) see the light of the ancient seed, pervading all like the day, that shines beyond, in the bright supreme Brahman.
4.2.3: Jānaśruti was not a śūdra by birth. With Śaṅkara, Raikva calls him so because grief (śuc) had seized him at the swans' words, or because he came for knowledge bringing only wealth, not service.
4.3.6: Śaṅkara takes kaḥ as Prajāpati, who is called Ka; some read it as a question: who is he?
4.3.7: Śaṅkara reads nedam as ā idam: we meditate on this; others read na idam: we meditate not on this but on the supreme Brahman.
4.3.8: With Śaṅkara, the first five are fire, the sun, the moon, the waters and air that swallows them; the other five are speech, the eye, the ear, the mind and prāṇa. In the kṛta throw four, three, two and one make ten; the Virāj metre has ten syllables, and the Veda calls Virāj food.
4.4.2: Śaṅkara explains that Jabālā was busy serving guests in her husband's house and never thought to ask his lineage, and that Satyakāma's father died at that time.
4.5.1: Śaṅkara takes the bull to be Vāyu, the deity of the quarters, speaking through it.
4.7.1: Śaṅkara takes the swan to be the sun, both being white and moving through the sky.
4.8.1: Śaṅkara takes the diver-bird, a water bird, to be prāṇa, because prāṇa is linked with water.
4.10.2: Śaṅkara reads paripravocan as reproach; others read it as: lest the fires teach him before you do.
4.10.5: Śaṅkara: ka and kha qualify each other, so the joy is not passing worldly pleasure and the space is not the inert element; the space of prāṇa is the space in the heart.
4.11.2: The usual sense of jyok is for a long time (he lives long); Śaṅkara takes it as brightly, not unknown. The phrase recurs in 4.12.2 and 4.13.2 in the same sense.
4.15.5: Śaṅkara takes the flame, the day and each stage after them as the deity presiding over it, who leads the traveller on, and the Brahman reached here as the Brahman of Brahmā's world (Satyaloka).
4.17.10: Śaṅkara reads kurūn as the performers of the sacrifice and mānava as the silent or reflective one; others take kurūn as the Kuru people.
5.3.7: Śaṅkara reads praśāsana as the teaching of this knowledge; others read it as the kṣatriyas' rule over all the worlds.
5.4.2: In Śaṅkara's reading, faith here is the subtle waters into which the agnihotra offerings have turned, and the gods are the sacrificer's prāṇas.
5.10.1: Śaṅkara takes those who know thus to be householders who know this teaching of the five fires, and the flame, the day and the rest to be the deities presiding over the stages of the path.
5.10.2: In Śaṅkara's reading this is Brahman with attributes, Hiraṇyagarbha, and the path ends in his world, Satyaloka.
5.10.4: Śaṅkara explains that the gods do not literally eat them: food here means what serves another's enjoyment, and they live happily with the gods as their attendants.
5.11.5: Śaṅkara explains that the sages had declined the wealth the king offered; thinking they saw some fault in him, he speaks of the purity of his realm, and then, thinking the gift was found too small, offers them a priest's share of his sacrifice.
5.18.1: This is Śaṅkara's reading of prādeśamātra and abhivimāna; others take prādeśamātra as a span in measure (from the head to the chin) and abhivimāna as immeasurable.
6.2.4: Here food stands, as Śaṅkara explains, for the element earth, whose form is food.
6.4.5: Śaṅkara takes naḥ, us, to mean our family; another reading is: now no one can name to us anything unheard, unthought or unknown.
6.8.2: Śaṅkara takes prāṇa here as Being, the highest deity, in which the mind, the individual self, rests in deep sleep; some read it as the breath itself.
6.14.2: The verbs vimokṣye and sampatsye are in the first person; Śaṅkara reads them as the third person, and being freed as the falling away of the body.
7.1.2: The sciences are named as Śaṅkara explains them: the Veda of the Vedas is grammar, pitrya the rites for the ancestors, rāśi mathematics, daiva the reading of portents, nidhi the science of treasures, vākovākya logic, ekāyana the science of conduct, devavidyā etymology, brahmavidyā phonetics, ritual, metre and the building of fire altars, kṣatravidyā archery, nakṣatravidyā astronomy, devajanavidyā perfumery, dance, song, music and crafts; modern scholars read several of these names otherwise.
7.5.3: Cittān is read with Śaṅkara as upacitān, built up and full of the qualities of the wise; taken as the participle of cit, it would be the worlds conceived by awareness.
7.20.1: Śaṅkara takes steadfastness (niṣṭhā) as devotion to serving the teacher and the like, for the sake of knowing Brahman.
7.21.1: Śaṅkara takes action (kṛti) as restraint of the senses and making the mind one-pointed.
7.26.2: Śaṅkara takes food (āhāra) as all that the senses take in, which is pure when untouched by attachment, aversion and delusion.
8.1.1: Śaṅkara: the city of Brahman is the body, the lotus-dwelling is the heart, and the inner space is Brahman itself.
8.3.3: Śaṅkara: the heavenly world here is Brahman in the heart, which all reach in deep sleep but only the knower reaches knowingly.
8.4.1: Śaṅkara takes cross here as reach: day and night and the rest do not reach the Self, and in the next mantra crossing the dam is reaching it.
8.5.3: Śaṅkara takes brahmaṇaḥ as Brahmā (Hiraṇyagarbha) and supplies hall with prabhuvimitaṃ hiraṇmayam, the golden hall built by Brahmā, the Lord.
8.6.5: Śaṅkara: the knower, meditating on the Self with Om, goes upward, the other goes sideways; the door of the world is the sun, through which one reaches the world of Brahman.
8.7.4: Śaṅkara: Prajāpati means the seer who sees through the eye; Indra and Virocana take him to mean the image reflected in the eye.
8.9.1: Srāma: one-eyed (or one whose eyes or nose keep running) in Śaṅkara's reading; the dictionaries give lame or sick.
8.13.1: Śaṅkara: the dark is Brahman in the heart, deep and hard to fathom; the many-coloured is the world of Brahman, rich in many joys.
8.14.1: Anuprāpatsi is in form an aorist, I have attained; Śaṅkara takes it as I wish to attain.
Śaṅkara takes the closing words to describe the female organ, red like a ripe jujube, which though toothless devours the vigour, strength and virtue of those who resort to it.
8.15.1: Tīrtha is usually a holy place; Śaṅkara takes it as what the scriptures permit.
